items.body:
Jysk brings unified commerce to UK&I and Ikea gets digital in China: last week’s biggest retail technology plays
RTIH rounds up the stand out retail technology deals, launches, deployments and pilots from the past seven days. Including Foot Locker, Morrisons, B&Q, Bluffworks, Frasers Group, Tesco Media, JULES, Footasylum, Fortenova Group, M&S, e.l.f. Cosmetics, and Ann Summers.
Foot Locker
Foot Locker has developed, in partnership with Stylitics, a new AI powered closet builder, Fits, within its mobile app. In a LinkedIn post, Michael Cera, Interim Head of Product Management and Design at Foot Locker, said: “AI is everywhere. But, at Foot Locker, we challenged ourselves to think about how to improve and make positive change to our customers shopping experience through the use of AI.”
He added: “We engaged with customers, really listened, and in partnership with Stylitics, developed a key new closet builder within the Foot Locker app - let me introduce you to Fits! Start with something you own. Discover personalised outfits built around it. See those looks come to life on a virtual model.”
Customers can upload or take a photo of something they own, discover complete outfits built around it, and visualise those looks on a virtual model. Paired with a cart addition from the model view, the aim is to make purchasing a whole outfit styled around your own products that much easier.
Cera concluded: “This was a collaborative effort across Experience Design, Product Management, E-comm, Brand, and Stylitics, and came to life exactly as we all set out to do. Download or open your Foot Locker app today and give it a try!”
B&Q
B&Q is ramping up its fast delivery push with the launch of TradePoint Express, a same-day delivery service exclusively for trade customers, in partnership with Gophr. The retailer has also expanded its Deliveroo partnership to more than 100 stores nationwide following a trial. Customers can now access up to more than 9,000 home improvement products through Deliveroo, with orders delivered in as little as 35 minutes.
The partnership with Gophr will allow Business Development Managers to arrange deliveries, either within two hours or for a pre-booked two-hour slot same-day, for TradePoint members from B&Q's standalone TradePoint store in Barking and 123 participating B&Q stores across the UK. The service is set to expand to all TradePoint stores later this year.
The launch builds on the introduction of Marketplace Click & Collect. Customers can now choose from an expanding range of collection and delivery options designed to suit planned projects, urgent repairs and last minute requirements.
Footasylum
THG Fulfil recently completed its first AutoStore implementation for an external retailer. Footasylum’s automated fulfilment operation is now live and delivering 212% of the output of the retailer’s previous operation, from fewer than half the picking stations.
Announced in June, the system processed its first customer order on 28th August and went fully live on 14th September. According to those involved, the build was delivered two months faster than the original project plan, with less than six months between contract signature and first order. A fleet of 85 AutoStore R5 robots operates across 96,000 bin locations, with 100% of Footasylum’s live SKU range stored in the grid and system uptime holding at 99.8%.
Before construction began, the two teams ran 80,000 simulations using Footasylum’s order history, seasonal demand curves and product data to determine the optimum number of robots and ports. At the heart of the live operation is THG Fulfil’s proprietary Warehouse Control System (WCS), developed over five years inside its own AutoStore network. Its in-house development team is refining the WCS after go-live, using live order data to improve bin sequencing, batching and stock positioning.
The project was delivered under a hybrid commercial model combining elements of capital investment and THG Fulfil’s robotics-as-a-service (RaaS) offering, structured specifically around Footasylum’s requirements.
Primepick
Primepick, a New York-based company that designs and manufactures robotic food kiosks, reports that it is expanding to new locations. The startup is bringing MealMate, an unattended kiosk that serves hot dishes in five to seven minutes, to a hospital and a nursing home in the Tri-State area, its fourth and fifth sites. Primepick is also preparing three new deployments in Huntsville, Chicago and Dallas.
These installations follow earlier ones at manufacturing sites in New Jersey and Connecticut and at Molloy University. For hospitals, manufacturing facilities and other round-the-clock environments, MealMate provides access to complete hot meals beyond traditional foodservice hours, without requiring an on-site kitchen or additional foodservice staff. At the aforementioned university, students order hot meals between classes and late into the evening, including dishes from local BBQ and Asian restaurants.
M&S
Klarna reports that it is now available as a payment option at Marks & Spencer for fashion, home and beauty purchases online. Shoppers on M&S.com and the UK retailer’s app can now tap Klarna and split the cost into three equal, interest free payments with, according to a press release, transparent terms and no revolving balance.
"People deserve flexibility without paying interest for it, so our goal is simple: meet them wherever they shop," says Klarna Head of UK, Ireland & Western & Southern Europe, Raji Behal. "M&S is a beloved British icon that brings second to none quality and value to millions of shoppers every day. We’re proud to now offer them a transparent way to spread the cost with no interest and a clear end date."
Katherine Carlson, Director of Financial Services at M&S, says: “We are always looking for ways to make it easier for our customers to shop with us. Customers shopping on M&S.com and through our app can now spread the cost in three interest free payments with Klarna, offering more flexibility in how they pay for the things they love.”
Orange
Pricer has been selected by Orange, a telecommunications operator in France, to digitalise its retail store network. The project encompasses 561 stores with an average size of 120 m² over the next two years.
The agreement covers the complete deployment of Pricer’s electronic shelf label (ESL) solution, including hardware, infrastructure, attachment solutions, installation, and cloud management via the Plaza platform under a long-term maintenance contract. It includes annual recurring SaaS and maintenance revenue. Orange chose Pricer following pilot programmes across multiple store locations.
Morrisons
Morrisons has selected Logile as it looks to enhance store workload planning across the UK grocery retailer’s business. The agreement covers its supermarket and convenience store estate alongside its logistics network.
Morrisons is implementing Logile software in a bid to simplify central planning, replacing time-consuming manual spreadsheets with optimised operational data and intelligence. By delivering clearer visibility into store workload requirements, it says that central operations can provide accurate, reliable insight across the estate, allowing teams to focus on better supporting store operations.
“Getting colleagues where customers need them most is the heart of what we do, and at our scale you need a reliable, shared foundation to get that right,” says Alex Rose, Head of Productivity at Morrisons. “A large supermarket and a local convenience store operate differently so our planning has to flex to those local needs while keeping central support consistent. When our store managers have plans they can depend on, they spend less time managing admin and more time supporting their colleagues and serving customers.”
Bluffworks
Travel apparel brand, Bluffworks, has selected Cart.com as its exclusive US fulfilment partner. Its inventory and fulfillment operations are now centralised at Cart.com’s Terrell, Texas facility. Bluffworks expects the new operation to lower its fulfilment costs by at least 20%.
"I've spent my career on both sides of logistics, first building supply chain systems as a software developer and then relying on them to run a brand," says Stefan Loble, Founder and CEO at Bluffworks. "I am still stunned at how different the accuracy, cost and level of service can be between two large, similar looking fulfilment providers.”
“Cart.com has their operation buttoned up, especially their technology. I can open their software and see the status of the whole operation without emailing anyone to ask. When something goes wrong, like a shipment turning up damaged, which happens in this business, you find out fast whether you’re in good hands on the other end. With Cart.com we are."
Ann Summers
InPost has partnered with Ann Summers with the retailer’s customers now able to choose 48-hour delivery to an InPost parcel locker at checkout, select a location and collect at a time that suits them. They will also be able to make returns through InPost’s network of over 16,000 lockers.
Jon Nicholson, Chief Commercial Officer, InPost UK, comments: “Ann Summers has spent decades disrupting the high street and empowering its customers, while InPost is challenging the way delivery has traditionally worked. Bringing those two mindsets together makes this a really exciting partnership. Customers expect choice throughout the shopping journey, and delivery should be no different.”
“By adding InPost locker delivery, Ann Summers is giving its customers greater freedom to choose the location and collection time that works best for them. For retailers, delivery is an increasingly important part of the overall customer experience. Giving people more options at checkout creates a more flexible, modern shopping journey, and that is exactly where InPost continues to push the category forward.”
Maria Hollins, CEO, Ann Summers, says: “For more than 50 years, we have pushed boundaries and championed empowerment, confidence and choice for our customers. Our partnership with InPost brings that same approach into another part of the shopping journey, giving our customers even greater freedom over how and where they receive their orders. We want every interaction with us to feel empowering and on our customers’ terms. InPost locker delivery gives them another simple and flexible option, putting even more choice into their hands.”
Fortenova Group
Hanshow, a Chinese specialist in digital store solutions, has partnered with Kenty Adria, a member of Fortenova Group, to support the large scale roll-out of electronic shelf labels (ESL) across Konzum and Mercator stores in Croatia and Slovenia. Building on pilot projects, the deployment forms part of the broader digital transformation of Fortenova Group's retail network.
At Konzum, electronic pricing has been introduced in more than 200 stores, with a further 260 stores planned for deployment. The largest implementation to date includes 44,000 electronic shelf labels installed at Konzum’s store on Radnička Street in Zagreb. The majority of its retail network, comprising more than 600 stores across Croatia, is expected to be equipped by the end of the 2027 summer season.
At Mercator, electronic shelf labels have so far been installed in 50 stores across Slovenia, with the goal of deploying ESL solutions throughout the entire Mercator retail network by the end of 2027. Across the network, the full roll-out is estimated to require approximately 3.1 million ESLs.
e.l.f. Cosmetics
e.l.f. Cosmetics, which is part of e.l.f. Beauty, has landed on ZEPETO, an avatar-based social metaverse platform. It has launched Express your e.l.f. where players can discover the beauty trends shaping culture and turn them into complete virtual looks from head to toe.
“As a different kind of company, e.l.f. does not see boundaries between where beauty lives and where culture happens. From Twitch to Roblox and now ZEPETO, we meet our community where they like to play and give them a platform to fuel discovery, empowerment and self-expression. Every immersive experience we build is an extension of the same vision that drives everything we do: disrupt norms, shape culture and connect communities through positivity, inclusivity and accessibility,” says Patrick O’Keefe, Chief Integrated Marketing Officer, e.l.f. Brands.
ZEPETO players can now dress their avatars in e.l.f. designed digital looks with makeup from the brand’s Power Grip family and hairstyles, bags, jewellery and special effects items inspired by Power Grip’s colours and textures. Players can also show off their e.l.f. looks by snapping photos and videos against custom backgrounds and sharing them to the ZEPETO feed.
“By seamlessly blending e.l.f. Cosmetics’ iconic products with the year’s most defining trends, ZEPETO is making it possible to reimagine makeup as a comprehensive head to toe virtual styling. We are thrilled to pioneer these full looks designed by e.l.f., delivering a revolutionary brand experience that pushes the boundaries of virtual self-expression,” says Annette Lee, Head of Business Development, ZEPETO.
Ikea
Ingka Group has launched an Ikea Douyin official flagship store in China. The new digital touchpoint will offer more than 6,500 Ikea products across 179 categories, with delivery available in 301 cities across China.
The move brings the retailer in to the short-form video and content commerce platform (a sister platform to TikTok under ByteDance). The store will complement its existing stores, website, app, WeChat and other e-commerce channels in China.
Lydia Song, Ikea China Acting CEO and President and CSO, says: “People in China are increasingly moving between inspiration, discovery and shopping in ways that are highly connected and increasingly digital. Douyin E-commerce gives us an opportunity to meet people in a new context, learn what resonates with them and make Ikea more accessible to more people. This is not simply about adding another sales channel. It is about understanding how we can become part of people’s everyday lives in new and relevant ways.”
Parag Parekh, Chief Digital Officer at Ikea Retail, comments: “Retail is increasingly about being present wherever and whenever people want to meet us, while making those experiences feel like one connected Ikea. What is particularly interesting about new platforms like Douyin E-commerce is the opportunity to learn. They help us understand how inspiration, interaction and commerce are coming closer together, and what that could mean for how we continue to develop the Ikea omnichannel experience.”
Jysk
Danish home furnishing retailer Jysk reports that the first of its UK and Ireland stores are now live with its Enactor powered unified commerce platform. In a LinkedIn post, Patrick Gretsch, Retail Operations Expert at Jysk, said: "Two more countries have taken their first steps towards a new way of working, with the first stores in the UK and Ireland now successfully running on our unified commerce platform."
"I had the pleasure of joining the team at our Sallynoggin store in Ireland to experience one of these first transitions firsthand. What stood out was the excellent preparation and collaboration across all departments involved. The result? A smooth and efficient changeover, completed while the store remained open and continued serving customers."
He added: "And this is just the beginning. The roll-out is progressing at pace, with all Jysk stores in both countries expected to be running on the new platform by mid-November. So, what does this mean for our colleagues and customers? For our store teams, unified commerce means simpler processes and new opportunities to serve customers directly on the shop floor. With mobile PoS, colleagues can process payments right where the customer interaction takes place, making the shopping experience more convenient and personal."
"For our customers, it opens the door to additional services. They can, for example, order products in a store and have them delivered directly coming from our warehouse straight to their doorstep. This is what makes unified commerce so exciting: it’s not just about introducing a new platform. It’s about improving the way we work and creating new opportunities to serve our customers."
Frasers Group
Frasers Group, whose brands include Sports Direct, House of Fraser, and Flannels, reports that Antrim in Northern Ireland has become the first of its warehouses to go live with a Microsoft Dynamics 365 warehouse management system (WMS).
In a LinkedIn post, Jakob Vestergaard, Product Manager - Warehouse at Frasers Group, said: "Two years of work. One major milestone. We're live. As the first warehouse in the group to adopt D365 WMS, Antrim marks an important milestone in our wider warehouse transformation journey."
"Over the last few years, Frasers Group has invested heavily in elevating our stores. This programme is about taking the next step by elevating the warehouse operations that power them, creating a more scalable, visible and consistent platform to support our stores, brands and customers. This achievement would not have been possible without the dedication of teams across the business and our partners."
He concluded: "Go live is a major achievement, but it isn't the end of the story. Over the coming months we'll continue working with our warehouse teams, Microsoft, Binary and InterRadish to refine the solution, introduce additional capabilities and build out the global warehouse template that will support future warehouse deployments across Frasers Group. This is the first step in a much bigger journey. Looking forward to what comes next."
Tesco Media
Tesco Media has unveiled a series of new capabilities designed to help brands turn deeper customer understanding into more helpful media experiences, more connected shopping journeys and clearer proof of growth. These were announced at its 2026 Upfront event.
Key here is Ad Manager, a new client facing platform designed to make planning, booking, measuring and optimising media simpler, more connected and more useful for brands. The self-service platform gives advertisers greater control and transparency over how they work with Tesco Media, while helping them turn customer insight into action with less complexity.
Tesco Media Ad Manager currently delivers Sponsored Products and will expand shortly into Display and Video as Tesco Media builds towards a more unified experience across its media ecosystem. Over time, AI powered workflows and recommendations will help advertisers reduce manual tasks, uncover new opportunities and make faster optimisation decisions, while greater interoperability will allow agencies and brands to connect the platform with the tools they already use.
The aim is to make control feel enabling rather than burdensome, giving brands simpler ways to create media that is timely, relevant and genuinely helpful to customers. The infrastructure behind Ad Manager is powered by Kevel, a specialist provider of API first ad technology for retailers and commerce media networks and designed to help Tesco Media deliver a seamless advertising experience across its digital channels.
JULES
JULES, a French menswear retailer with over 350 stores across France and owned by Association Familiale Mulliez, has selected Ekinops solutions as it looks to modernise web security and better support its evolving digital usage.
Based in Roubaix and employing 2,800 people, JULES was looking for a replacement solution capable of providing greater visibility into internet usage, making filtering policies easier to manage and strengthening employee protection against web-based risks, without compromising user experience.
It says it selected Ekinops’ solution for its performance, ease of integration into the existing information system, its ability to facilitate the migration of filtering rules, the quality of website categorisation and the availability of clear dashboards enabling more effective monitoring of usage, blocks and risks. Ekinops’ positioning as a French software provider was also an important criterion, in line with requirements for sovereignty, proximity, GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) compliance and trust in data management.
Morrisons
Just Eat is expanding its autonomous delivery robot trial with Starship Technologies to Cambourne in Cambridgeshire. This is the first trial location where it doesn't already offer grocery delivery and builds on Sunderland and Milton Keynes deployments.
Morrisons has become one of the first grocery brands to tap the technology, with benefits including adding delivery capacity in the run up to the festive season and during offers such as the regular 'Half Price Wednesdays' on Just Eat. The Cambourne supermarket which is now live is the fourth Morrisons to begin autonomous robot deliveries with three Morrisons Dailys live across Sunderland and Milton Keynes.
THG Commerce
THG Commerce, part of THG Ingenuity, has integrated Criteo Sponsored Products into its AI Shopping Assistant, built using Google Cloud’s Gemini Enterprise. THG Commerce says it is the first commerce technology provider in Europe to bring Criteo Sponsored Products into AI powered conversational search, opening up a new retail media opportunity for retailers and brands.
Retailers can now monetise customer conversations through relevant sponsored product placements. The integration places sponsored and organic product recommendations side by side within the same conversation. Brands can reach shoppers in AI driven discovery moments, when intent is high and recommendations are shaped by the shopper's own words. Early results show sponsored products surfaced through the AI Shopping Assistant reached a click-through rate more than five times the average, and a conversion rate more than double the average.
The AI Shopping Assistant draws keywords and filters from each conversation and turns them into tailored product recommendations. When a Criteo Sponsored Product is eligible and relevant, it appears clearly labelled within the assistant's response alongside organic recommendations, adding to the discovery experience rather than interrupting it.
The same relevance models that power Criteo search advertising, including keyword matching, semantic understanding and strict relevance thresholds, apply in the conversational context. Sponsored recommendations appear only when they match what the shopper has asked for.
The integration builds on THG Ingenuity’s broader partnership with Criteo and on its wider collaboration with Google Cloud. THG Commerce has developed a suite of agentic commerce solutions built on Gemini Enterprise. Alongside the AI Shopping Assistant, these include the AI Stylist, which offers AI powered virtual try-on for beauty, apparel and footwear, and Shopping Assistant Insights, which is available in Gemini Enterprise and helps retailers understand what their shoppers want and how the assistant is serving them. Each is delivered as a plug and play SaaS service, available through Google Cloud Marketplace and able to operate independently of the underlying storefront.

AI powered marketing platform Miracly publicly launches with $2 million pre-seed funding round
Miracly, a GEO and AI operating system for marketing teams and agencies developed by The Wild Ventures, the company behind Scandinavian home decor brand Wild Palace, has announced a $2 million pre-seed round led by Beenext Ventures and Lotus alongside a Swedish family office, with existing investors including Stefan Lindeberg, Founder at VC firm Creandum; Alex Bouaziz, Founder and CEO at Deel; Thomas Ekman, Founder at 6GAI and former CEO at Axel Johnson publ, Dustin and Tele2; Hedda Baverud Olsson, Founder and CEO at Lassie, and Parham Benisi, Partner at Pophouse.
The company publicly launched last week. Pre-launch it has landed customers including Dreams, Acclime, Pixi Beauty, Andy Okay and Duellix.
“We’re seeing an incredible demand for Miracly’s AI marketing platform. Companies all over the world are impacted by decreasing organic traffic from Google and increasing cost of performance marketing,” says Bjorn Bergstrom, Co-founder at Miracly.
“We started out with GEO analytics and AI content generation, but are rapidly becoming a holistic AI marketing platform based on the demand and opportunity we’re seeing in the market. Marketing and agency teams are becoming hybrid marketing and tech organisations and need to develop incredibly quickly to keep up with the changes. Miracly is here to guide them through this shift into an AI first era with completely customised recommendations and agentic flows.”
Vestiaire Collective becomes first luxury resale platform to standardise new listing photos with AI
Photoroom has published results from its work with Vestiaire Collective, a platform for pre-loved luxury fashion. Vestiaire Collective split its new listings into two random groups. One had its main photo edited by Photoroom, the other by the photo clipping tool Vestiaire Collective built in-house years ago. Listings in the Photoroom group sold at a 5% higher rate of liquidity. Their product pages drew 3 to 7% more unique views, with bags and shoes gaining the most.
Vestiaire Collective says it chose Photoroom after testing several generative AI tools and finding that every one of them changed the items. A photo that changes the item breaks two things on a resale platform. Vestiaire Collective authenticates a share of items from their photos alone, checking labels, stitching and how light falls on the material. Buyers can also return anything that turns out to be fake or has a fault the seller didn't disclose. Smooth out a scuff or redraw a logo and both are at risk.
Photoroom's own testing points the same way. In a benchmark of 4,250 AI generated images across 850 real products, the best AI image editing models on the market passed a full product fidelity check only 29% of the time. 63% of UK consumers say inconsistent product images or branding make a marketplace less trustworthy, according to Photoroom's State of GenAI in Marketplaces 2026 report.
Tomáš Čupr bags $32 million for Duvo, an AI platform born from challenges he encountered while building Rohlik
Duvo, an automation platform that gives teams an AI workforce for their day-to-day operations, has announced a $32 million Series A led by Balderton Capital, with participation from existing investors Index Ventures, Northzone and Credo Ventures. The round brings its total funding to $48 million and will fund its expansion, starting with retailers and CPG companies.
Michael Green is also joining from Databricks as Senior Vice President, Go-to-Market. He previously served as a Senior Vice President at Salesforce. Spencer Insolia recently came onboard as Managing Director, US. He was previously President at Kmart and a Managing Director at Accenture. Christoph Schwaiger, former CEO at Aldi South Holdings, has also signed on as Senior Advisor for Europe.
"For a while I measured AI in heads, counting how many people an agent could replace. It's the wrong unit," says Tomáš Čupr, Co-founder and CEO at Duvo and Founder and Group CEO at Rohlik Group. "At Rohlik, the gains I'd point to came from work nobody had the hours for. Our planners used to check about eight at-risk products a day per market for shortages. Now every signal gets checked, around the clock. We think of it as raising the GDP of every employee: more value from the people a company has, not the same value from fewer of them."
Kingfisher raids European home improvement retailer OBI to bring in Sebastian Gundel as CEO
Kingfisher, which owns B&Q and Screwfix in the UK and Castorama and Brico Depot in France and other markets, has announced the appointment of Sebastian Gundel as Chief Executive Officer, effective 1st February 2027. He will join Kingfisher’s board of directors on the same date.
He brings more than two decades of leadership experience in the home improvement sector, including as Chief Executive Officer at European retailer OBI, where he led the company's evolution from traditional retail to a digitally enabled, customer centric, omnichannel business.
Prior to becoming CEO, he served as Chief Customer & Digital Officer, leading OBI's omnichannel transformation and digital innovation agenda. His responsibilities spanned loyalty, marketplaces and ecosystem development, as well as the expansion of trade propositions.
Claudia Arney, Chair, says: “Following a thorough selection process, the board is delighted to appoint Sebastian as Chief Executive Officer. Sebastian combines deep experience in home improvement retail and clear expertise in Kingfisher’s strategic growth drivers with a strong track record of innovation and operational delivery. items.body:
Pixel Inspiration and dunnhumby deliver Sony BRAVIA powered retail media roll-out for Booker Wholesale
Booker Wholesale has deployed more than 500 Sony BRAVIA Professional Displays to establish a new retail media network across 100 of its UK locations. The project was delivered by Pixel Inspiration in partnership with dunnhumby.
Installed predominantly at rack ends and above palletised merchandise, the displays provide a platform for targeted advertising and promotional content, while integrating into the existing wholesale environment. This presented specific challenges for the installation. Displays needed to be positioned for maximum visibility while also being protected against accidental impacts from stock movement, pallet handling and day-to-day warehouse operations.
Sony BZ35L BRAVIA Professional Displays were selected as part of the hardware solution to provide the combination of image quality, reliability and operational efficiency required for the network. To provide additional protection, Pixel Inspiration worked with UNICOL to develop a combined mounting and protective shroud solution. This was designed to withstand the demands of a busy cash and carry environment while maintaining appropriate airflow and ventilation around the displays.
The displays use Sony’s Android-based System on Chip (SoC) technology, reducing the need for additional external media players and helping simplify the overall installation. The network is managed through the DISE content management system, enabling campaign content to be centrally targeted and distributed across Booker’s national estate.
Sony Remote Device Manager is also used to monitor the displays remotely, carry out firmware updates and undertake maintenance tasks. This helps reduce the need for onsite intervention and supports efficient management of the large scale display network.
“Booker’s nationwide retail media network is a great example of how digital signage is evolving to create new opportunities for brands to engage customers in highly relevant environments," says Karl Ingham, Key Account Manager, Sony Professional Displays and Solutions Europe.
"This deployment demonstrates the scalability and versatility of Sony’s display technology, while the combination of high quality visuals, remote device management and reliable performance makes it well suited to the demands of a busy wholesale environment. We’re delighted to support Booker and Pixel Inspiration in creating a platform that can deliver value for both Booker’s customers and its brand partners."

H&M Home reopens flagship store on Drottninggatan with new global store concept and visual identity
H&M Home has reopened its flagship store at Drottninggatan 50 in Stockholm, Sweden following an extensive renovation. The 383 sq m location will be the first Home offering globally to showcase the retailer’s new store concept and updated visual identity.
It is designed as a series of connected rooms that guide customers through different areas of the home, from social spaces such as the living and dining room to more personal settings including the bedroom and bathroom.
“H&M Home is constantly evolving, while staying true to its core. We want to preserve the warm and welcoming character that customers associate with the brand, while refining and modernising our expressions. At Drottninggatan, this comes to life through a new store concept where materials, scale and carefully curated environments work together to create an experience that feels both contemporary and timeless. It reflects the direction we will continue to develop for H&M Home, with design, quality and the home at its heart,” says Evelina Kravaev-Söderberg, Head of Design & Creative at H&M Home.
“Drottninggatan is a strategically important destination for Home and a natural home for our Swedish flagship store. The new store represents the future of Home and a clearer expression of the brand. Home is aspirational and inspiring, while always remaining close to customers’ everyday lives. We look forward to welcoming both local and international visitors to a store that sets the standard for Home going forward,” says Frida Dahlquist, General Manager at H&M Home.
The store will also continue to offer Home’s monogramming service, allowing customers to personalise selected products, as well as an integrated florist concept in partnership with Bunchery.

items.title: Retail brands expanding cross-border: the people problem nobody budgets for
items.summary: Retail expansion plans tend to be built around property, stock and logistics. Lease terms, fit-out costs and supply chains are costed in considerable detail, with contingencies in case they overrun. The people who will run the new operation, however, often get far less attention. In practice, staffing, payroll and local employment law are core to every new store or online launch, and they usually take longer and cost more than first expected. Why Staffing a New Market Is Rarely as Simple as Hiring Locally A new market needs more than shopfloor staff. Appointing experienced store managers, making changes to e-commerce logistics and supporting the customer service team should all be considered, often before the brand has a legal presence in the country. Notice periods, probation frameworks and employment contracts vary by jurisdiction, so a template approach copied from what works in the original country or region may not be valid. Recruitment also needs to be adapted to the local market
items.body:
Retail brands expanding cross-border: the people problem nobody budgets for
Retail expansion plans tend to be built around property, stock and logistics. Lease terms, fit-out costs and supply chains are costed in considerable detail, with contingencies in case they overrun. The people who will run the new operation, however, often get far less attention.
In practice, staffing, payroll and local employment law are core to every new store or online launch, and they usually take longer and cost more than first expected.
Why Staffing a New Market Is Rarely as Simple as Hiring Locally
A new market needs more than shopfloor staff. Appointing experienced store managers, making changes to e-commerce logistics and supporting the customer service team should all be considered, often before the brand has a legal presence in the country.
Notice periods, probation frameworks and employment contracts vary by jurisdiction, so a template approach copied from what works in the original country or region may not be valid. Recruitment also needs to be adapted to the local market. Salary benchmarks, candidate management and typical benefits may need extra attention to attract experienced people and keep offers in line with local laws and industry regulations.
How Seasonal and Temporary Hiring Rules Change From Country to Country
Seasonal peaks add more pressure because retail relies on temporary and fixed term workers, and these contracts are often tightly regulated. The OECD’s employment protection indicators compare countries’ rules on dismissal and temporary contracts, and those rules differ considerably. A seasonal staffing model that works in one country may be restricted in another, whether through rules on agency workers or the cost of ending a contract.
The Payroll and Benefits Obligations That Arrive With the First Hire
Once someone is employed, the employer must register with the local tax and social security authorities, calculate deductions, issue payslips and make regular filings. Pensions, health contributions, holiday pay and sick pay are set locally, so it’s vital to understand what applies where.
In retail, shift patterns and hours can change week to week, so accurate handling of pay and overtime is essential. For a company running payroll in several countries, separate providers and spreadsheets can quickly produce inconsistent reporting and limited visibility of the true cost.
Local Employment Law and the Cost of Getting It Wrong
Working hours, overtime, minimum wage, rest breaks and trading day rules, including Sunday working, differ by country and sometimes by region. Entering through a franchise partner can shift much of this burden, an approach we noted when lululemon entered Romania. Brands that operate their own stores, or hire head office and retail staff directly, take those obligations on themselves, which can increase the risk of getting things wrong.
Options for Employing Staff Before a Local Entity Exists
Setting up a subsidiary takes time and money, and it is not always justified for a test market. One alternative is an employer of record (EOR), which becomes the legal employer in the country, handling contracts, payroll and statutory contributions while the company controls the day-to-day work. This can suit new markets, pop-ups and early head office roles.
Providers such as GoGlobal offer EOR services alongside entity establishment, global payroll and broader HR services in more than 100 countries, so a retailer can start with one arrangement and move to another as the market grows. The trade off is that an EOR is usually a transitional structure, and brands expecting sustained local trading will eventually need to reconsider which structure suits their current stage.
What to Build Into the Budget Before Opening in a New Market
A people budget for a new market should typically account for:
- Recruitment and onboarding, including any head office roles
- Payroll, benefits and health contributions
- Legal and HR advice on contracts and working restrictions
- The cost of changing structure later, such as moving from an EOR to an owned entity
Treating these as key expenses rather than afterthoughts gives finance and operations teams a more realistic view of what a new market will cost, long before the first retail store opens.

items.title: World leaders must wise up to threat of cyber-attacks or rogue fridges will be least of their worries | Heather Stewart
items.summary: Global cooperation seems unlikely despite AI increasing the risk of digital fraud and the need to protect the financial system Rogue French fridges were an unlikely talking point for the world’s leading economists, central bankers and finance chiefs meeting in a sultry Bangkok last week – helping to underline the spiralling cost of cyber-attacks. Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the International Monetary Fund, seized on news that supermarket chains across France had to chuck out piles of spoiled food after hackers accessed their fridge controls and turned up the temperature to 50C. Continue reading...
items.body:
Rogue French fridges were an unlikely talking point for the world’s leading economists, central bankers and finance chiefs meeting in a sultry Bangkok last week – helping to underline the spiralling cost of cyber-attacks.
Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the International Monetary Fund, seized on news that supermarket chains across France had to chuck out piles of spoiled food after hackers accessed their fridge controls and turned up the temperature to 50C.
Speaking at the fund’s annual meetings in the Thai capital, she was keen to hammer home the importance of guarding against “bad actors” in a rapidly changing, interconnected world – especially now that AI was “putting the potential of digital fraud on steroids”.
Policymakers have been warning for some time that the AI boom could at some point threaten financial stability via a share price crash – a “correction”, as it is euphemistically called.
But a different, related threat came into sharp focus in Bangkok. Georgieva said she was concerned that cybercrime, turbocharged by AI, could undermine trust in the financial system altogether.
Social media feeds are rife with adverts using celebrity fakes to punt cryptocurrencies or gold, and even the old-school email-style scams can be generated far more prolifically.
Just as a sea of AI slop has the potential to undermine trust in fact-based reporting and send people down political rabbit holes, Georgieva fretted that cyber-fraud could knock consumer confidence in mainstream banks.
Recalling her own childhood behind the iron curtain in Bulgaria, she said many people did not trust the system, and kept their cash in a shoebox under the bed. “I worry, today, that unless we figure out how to get ahead of this curve … we may end up with lots of people with shoeboxes under their beds,” she said.
It might not even take a cybercrime wave. This week the JP Morgan chief executive, Jamie Dimon, warned that the bank would not allow digital agents to operate on its customers’ behalf. “You don’t want rogue agents, and there could be thousands of them,” he said.
AI agents, including Meta’s Muse, are starting to offer their users the opportunity to hand over their financial details. The agents will then scout for the highest savings rates and shift the user’s money accordingly.
Financial regulators fret about this for a number of reasons. One is that if such services become widely used, they could have destabilising herding effects. With deposits able to be moved around the financial system at a moment’s notice, it could accelerate a bank run in times of uncertainty.
A second worry is that highlighted by Dimon: who is responsible if your AI agent makes a financial decision on your behalf that turns out to be disastrous – or even criminal?
The answer is probably that we will need case law to find out, which will only come when something goes badly awry.
That is alarming because legal ambiguity about who owes what to whom when things go wrong can be an accelerant to financial instability.
We learned that lesson back in the 2008 financial crisis, when it turned out that some banks had built financial products with such fiendishly complex liability structures that they were effectively impossible to value – unleashing panic.
Speaking alongside Georgieva, the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, who chairs the Financial Stability Board of global central bankers, pointed to another arresting news story from this week – that Anthropic had warned AI models might soon be able to “self-replicate” in domestic devices. Who should bear the responsibility – and the costs – if your internet-enabled oven, or telly, blows up as a result?
One entirely prudent response might be for consumers to reject internet-enabled devices and stick to “dumb” appliances instead that can’t be hijacked by self-replicating bots. This month, some of those French supermarkets rushed to take their fridges offline to avoid the hack.
While it may not be much of a loss to society if internet-enabled kettles and fridges do not take off, the financial analogue to a dumb appliance would be Georgieva’s shoeboxes – and that would have costs for those consumers, and the smooth running of the economy as a whole.
As Bailey somewhat apocalyptically put it: “If we don’t have trust in money, we don’t operate as a society.”
Senior financial policymakers are genuinely disturbed at the collision between rapidly developing AI and the global financial system – which now extends well beyond heavily regulated banks – to embrace social media platforms, payments apps and other financial tools.
It is unfortunate this moment comes as the US – the crucible of the AI boom – is governed by a man whose main contribution to the debate has been to seek to rename AI “superintelligence”.
At the Bangkok meetings this week, Kevin Warsh, the chair of the US Federal Reserve, obediently used Donald Trump’s phrase on stage – as all US government agencies have been ordered to.
There has been some progress in acknowledging the risks. Trump’s superintelligence taskforce, chaired by the director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, is setting up mechanisms for AI labs to report “breaches, hacks, jailbreaks, and other issues” – although not, it seems, to submit their models for pre-launch testing.
The UK has pledged to take up the issue of AI safety as part of its agenda for the G20 presidency next year, and G7 finance ministers announced in Bangkok that they would carry out simulations to test the resilience of the global financial system to cyber-attacks.
That could help to highlight vulnerabilities, but the questions at stake are much wider and more complex than whether criminals can hack the banks – and are urgent now, just as the prospects for international cooperation seem bleak. Superintelligence will seem anything but super if its misuse becomes a trigger for financial chaos.

items.title: My historic hotel in Devon inspired an Agatha Christie hit: John Healey must give businesses like mine a discount on business rates
items.summary: Giles Fuchs, whose Burgh Island art deco hotel in Devon inspired Agatha Christie's thriller And Then There Were None, is calling for sites like his to receive a 5% discount on business rates.
items.body:
My historic hotel in Devon inspired an Agatha Christie hit: John Healey must give businesses like mine a discount on business rates
Historic pubs and hotels are urging the Chancellor John Healey for a discount on their business rates in order to protect heritage sites.
There are tens of thousands of hospitality venues operating in listed buildings in England and Wales, according to official figures.
Pubs and small music venues have benefited from lower business rates promised by Prime Minister Andy Burnham from next year, but many historic hospitality sites face higher bills.
They also have to pay the standard 20 percent VAT on the upkeep and repair of the buildings themselves, including ensuring architecturally important elements are protected.
The owner of the luxury hotel that inspired Agatha Christie is one of such listed buildings.
Giles Fuchs, whose Burgh Island art deco hotel in Devon inspired Agatha Christie's thriller And Then There Were None, is calling for sites like his to receive a 5 per cent discount on business rates to preserve Britain's heritage sites and encourage tourism.
Time for a break: Historic pubs and hotels are urging the Chancellor John Healey for a discount on their business rates in order to protect heritage sites
'Too many businesses are being caught between a rock and a hard place,' because of rising employment and energy costs, he said.
'For those operating from listed buildings, that challenge is even greater,' he added.
Giles Fuchs owns the Burgh Island art deco hotel in Devon, which inspired Agatha Christie's thriller And Then There Were None
'They are expected to protect and maintain nationally important properties, often at considerable cost and with strict limitations on the changes they can make, yet there is very little recognition of that responsibility in the tax system.'
His hotel has more than 200 Crittall windows with original metal from the 1930s that can't withstand the sea air.
They cost around £10,000 each to refurbish - compared to £2,000-3,000 for the modern equivalent.
Fuchs added: 'These historic hotels, pubs and venues are bastions of British history and the soul of so many local communities.
'They are places where generations have gathered, worked, celebrated and made memories, and once they are lost, they cannot simply be replaced.
'As custodians, we have a responsibility not only to protect them today, but to leave something behind for those who come after us.
'Sensible business rates relief would help safeguard these buildings, support the hospitality businesses that keep them alive and ensure that future generations can continue to experience the history, hospitality, character and sense of place that make Britain so distinctive.'

I shut The Works website to focus on shops instead - and the High Street is paying off, reveals boss Gavin Peck
items.summary: Gavin Peck knows something is wrong if he visits one of his shops and doesn't bring anything home for his young daughters.
items.body:
I shut The Works website to focus on shops instead - and the High Street is paying off, reveals boss Gavin Peck
Gavin Peck knows something is wrong if he visits one of his shops and doesn’t bring anything home for his young daughters.
It means what’s on offer has ‘got a bit stale’, says the boss of discount retailer The Works.
But recently, Peck, 45 this month, has been returning with two or three bags full of goodies.
He says: ‘They run to the door, “Daddy’s home, where’s our treats?” they demand.’
It suggests The Works – whose yellow branded shops have become a staple of many shopping malls since it was founded in 1981 – is getting it right. But times are tough – as they are for most retailers.
Affordability is key with cash-strapped shoppers set to feel the squeeze even more when energy bills soar this winter.
The Works, which has more than 500 shops in the UK and Ireland, offers ‘dupes’ of popular, but pricey toys such as Lego and Labubus, the viral collectible monster figures. Do children care it’s not the real thing? Yes, maybe, Peck concedes, but it’s not them buying.
Gavin Peck knows something is wrong if he visits one of his shops and doesn’t bring anything home for his young daughters
When Peck joined as chief executive in 2020, the business had a reputation of ‘piling it high and selling it cheap’. It has since ‘worked really hard’ to broaden its appeal.
This includes making shops ‘more inviting’ – ‘you wouldn’t have been able to get a buggy around our shop five years ago’, he admits – and stocking more ‘relevant products, not just old clearance stuff that people didn’t want.’
Peck is trying to appeal to a TikTok-savvy generation, which will also make for the retailer’s ‘best Christmas ever’, he insists.
What about books, where the business began? Well, they take up less space than they used to in shops – but they’re still big sellers.
The brand has moved to top-selling titles. Peck says: ‘We wouldn’t have had Richard Osman in three or four years ago.’
Its market share on books is 11 per cent by volume, sitting with Waterstones and travel retailer WHSmith in the top three biggest bricks-and-mortar book retailers in the UK.
New titles set to do well include the sixth in fantasy writer Sarah J Maas’s A Court Of Thorns And Roses series and psychological thriller The Witch by Freida McFadden.
The retailer has started stocking Pokemon cards, after not selling them due to fears over staff safety. The trading cards craze is so rampant they are a target for criminal gangs. A bigger issue is what he calls ‘nuisance theft’.
One of Peck’s biggest changes was shutting The Works’ website in March to focus on shops. It may go against the shift to online, but he says it has been a ‘real positive’ with evidence that online customers have been heading into stores.
He says the website was ‘becoming a distraction’ given the challenge of selling low-priced items. He is upbeat about no longer having to compete with online giants and says it hasn’t stopped growth.
He adds: ‘Kids want to come in and touch and feel the product.’
Peck is among those asking ministers to crack down on a customs duty loophole that lets foreign online retailers, including China’s Shein and Temu, dodge paying tax on cheap parcels sent to the UK. The Government has pledged to do this before October 2028, but retailers say this is far too late.
‘If that could happen quicker, that would level the playing field a little bit,’ Peck says, and hits out at the deluge of unregulated products flooding into the UK.
‘When customers buy from us, they can have the confidence that it’s going to be a good-quality product, it’s going to be safe, and we are subject to regulations.’
He is also pushing an array of ‘screen-free activities’ for children. As the Government moves to ban social media for under-16-year-olds, it is a pertinent issue.
But, as a parent, he knows that often the ‘easiest thing’ to do is to put a child ‘in front of an iPad’.
The Works was embroiled in a boardroom bust-up this summer
Peck’s first experience in retail was helping his aunt and uncle with their Spar franchise with his cousins in the school holidays.
‘We used to do stock takes and when we finished about midnight, we used to do trolley races around the shop – that was fun,’ he recalls.
After training as an accountant and working in corporate finance, Peck joined Card Factory, becoming commercial director.
He says: ‘I’ve never been that excited about just putting a set of accounts together, that side of finance, but understanding how the business operates, how it ticks, and what makes it work was a great grounding.’
Growing up in a large family, with ‘huge Christmases’ and now being a dad, has also helped give him perspective for the business.
He says: ‘Having the kids who are at that age living and breathing our products, gives me a really good sense of our products.’
Like others, Peck is frustrated by the lack of action on business rates, which he says can be higher than rents for some shops.
Another distraction was a boardroom bust-up this summer involving The Works’ board and activist investor Kelso, which holds 10 per cent of the retailer. Kelso accused The Works’ chairman Steve Bellamy of not spending enough time in the UK and dialling into board meetings from New Zealand.
It wanted to install a former Card Factory director to the board but the plan was defeated at The Works’ annual general meeting.
In his first public comments since, Peck said he was pleased investors had backed the board.
‘Kelso are a sizeable shareholder and we will keep engaging with them going forwards’, he said. ‘But for now, that is behind us.’

items.title: Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?
items.summary: Whether it was youngsters proving their skills or state sabotage, Europe’s most hacked country was left with a mountain of waste after food began cooking in freezers Shortly before midnight last Sunday, the digital thermostats controlling hundreds of supermarket cold aisles across France began to flicker and rise. In a “bizarre and unprecedented” cyber-attack, hackers had remotely overridden the temperature settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F). Continue reading...
items.body:
Shortly before midnight last Sunday, the digital thermostats controlling hundreds of supermarket cold aisles across France began to flicker and rise.
In a “bizarre and unprecedented” cyber-attack, hackers had remotely overridden the temperature settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F).
Over the next four to six hours, the food inside first defrosted, then slowly began to cook.
Shop staff arriving early to restock shelves reported catching a blast of hot air, like opening an oven, when they went to fill freezers. One Normandy supermarket reported a number of its freezers had been pushed to 80C (176F). In certain stores, the extreme temperature rise had sparked fires triggering sprinklers and water damage.
“It was a catastrophe,” said one worker at the large Intermarché supermarket in the south-west suburb of Issy-les-Moulineaux in Paris. “They pushed the freezers here up to 62C. Everything had to be thrown away. It was such a waste.”
After removing tons of spoiled food, staff at the store worked until almost midnight on Monday to reorder and restock shelves. “Thankfully, we were able to get things almost back to normal the same day,” another shop worker added. “But we had to clear out everything in the freezers.”
If shop managers first assumed it was an isolated failure, it soon became clear up to 700 stores – including those from the Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains along with a number of smaller independent shops – had been victims of a cyber-attack.
Dominique Schelcher, the president of Coopérative U, said 80 of its 2,000 supermarkets had been targeted. “This is a completely unprecedented, unexpected, and extremely serious attack. In my entire professional career, I’ve never seen anything like it,” the shocked executive told French radio.
The Paris public prosecutor’s office immediately opened an investigation into the latest in a series of cyber-attacks that have made France the most hacked country in Europe.
Gérôme Billois, a partner in the cybersecurity and technology company Wavestone, said the hack had the hallmarks of political sabotage.
“The two most feasible scenarios are either it was a group of youngsters or activists who wanted to blow up a few freezers to prove what they could do, or it was a destabilising attack, what we call sabotage, by internal or external state actors,” he said.
“As for the attack’s signature, the most likely scenario is still a destabilisation attack – one designed to convey the message to populations that they are not safe, to convey the impression that the government is falling apart, and ultimately to instil fear.
“Currently there are two international actors known for doing this sort of thing: Iran and Russia.”
The hackers had pirated the controllers supplied by the Danish company Danfoss that controls the freezers and fridges. Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. Initial investigations suggest the hackers disabled alarm systems before tampering with the thermostats, or extended the defrost programme by several hours to avoid triggering alarms.
Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” that customers install updates or replace obsolete unsupported systems. The affected refrigeration units were “running outdated firmware”, it said. In the days following the first wave of attacks, France’s cyber-attack alert centre ANSSI confirmed supermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted.
Marta Rybczyńska, a cybersecurity specialist and researcher, said she had found previous security warnings about old supermarket freezers running out-of-date software and newer models not having firmware updated.
“Some of these freezers hadn’t been supported by the manufacturers for several years and there were notices saying they should be replaced. Other freezers were newer but the software hadn’t been updated,” Rybczyńska said.
“The hackers found these weaknesses and used them.”
She added: “Many of the freezers appear to have been running with a default password. The hackers were able to modify or turn off the alerts so the shops only realised when the first person arrived in the morning and saw the damage that had been done.”
The most recent French cyber-attack mirrors a similar incident in the US in August when connected fridges and freezers at a dozen military commissaries – on-base food stores – went into unscheduled defrost cycles overnight causing massive food loss.
France is the most heavily pirated country in Europe by the volume of records exposed by hackers, according to the cybersecurity and risk management company Upguard.
In the last three years, hackers have breached France’s health system, France Travail, the government-run jobseekers agency, the National Agency for Identity Documents (ANTS) and most of the big mobile phone companies. This summer, the economy and finance ministry lost the personal and fiscal records of 678,000 taxpayers to a series of cyber-attacks.
Billois says France has fallen behind in addressing cybersecurity and has still not adopted the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act (2024) that introduced mandatory security for internet-connected devices.
“It’s a text that’s not political and that everyone agrees on but is delayed because there’s always more urgent legislation or there are quibbles about amendments, and this has been a disaster,” he said.
In the UK, the cyber security and resilience (network and information systems) bill to tackle cyber threats, is wending a similarly tortuous way through parliament. However, it fails to directly cover the food industry.
Supermarket boss Schelcher was quick to shift the blame for the attack on to unnamed refrigeration contractors who maintain the cold aisle equipment. “Our supermarkets are not customers of Danfoss,” he told RTL radio.
As yet, no individual or group has claimed responsibility for the supermarket cyber-attack; Paris prosecutors have instructed detectives from its anti-cybercrime unit but Billois says finding the hackers will take time.
“It’s possible they’ll be identified eventually, but it could take weeks if not months to be certain because hackers know how to hide their tracks,” Billois said.
Rybczyńska added: “Whether it’s possible to trace the hackers depends on their level of capability; if it’s a handful of youngsters, it’s easier because they probably won’t have thought to remove traces. If they are professionals it’s more complicated and will take longer. If they’re in a foreign country, it’ll be extremely difficult.”
The total cost of the cyber-attack has yet to be calculated but Thierry Cotillard, the CEO of Intermarché, said losses could run to “tens of millions of euros”, which store companies say is unlikely to be covered by their insurance.
“It’s a bizarre story,” Billois added. “There’s a shared responsibility between the supermarkets, the refrigeration companies who are sub-contractors and who maintain the material, and the software company. We cannot say who is to blame except, of course, the hackers.
“But in the end it comes down to freezers connected to the internet without being adequately secured. And that must be a wake-up call to everyone.”

items.title: ACS urges retailers to get involved with ShopKind Week 2026
items.summary: The Association of Convenience Stores (ACS) is encouraging retailers to get involved with ShopKind Week, beginning on 9 November this year. ShopKind is a campaign within the retail sector that aims to raise awareness about violence towards shopworkers, while acknowledging the essential role of shopworkers… This story continues at ACS urges retailers to get involved with ShopKind Week 2026 Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
ShopKind is a campaign within the retail sector that aims to raise awareness about violence towards shopworkers, while acknowledging the essential role of shopworkers and reminding customers to “shop kind” when visiting stores.
Figures from the 2026 ACS Crime Report found that there were over 67,000 estimated incidents of violence towards shopworkers, and almost a million incidents of verbal abuse.
The ACS is encouraging retailers to spread the ShopKind message by:
- Sharing #ShopKind assets on social media
- Putting ShopKind posters up in their stores
- Getting staff to wear ShopKind badges
- Nominating someone from their business to be a ShopKind Champion
Free materials are available on the National Business Crime Centre website.
ACS chief executive Ed Woodall said: “Shopworkers and convenience retailers have the right to feel safe when they are serving their communities and should never be subject to abuse.
“This campaign acts as a reminder to all customers that it is important to treat everyone with kindness and respect.”
For the first time, ShopKind Week will form part of a wider co-ordinated campaign to promote staff safety messages.
The week of action will also include the National Business Crime Centre’s Safer Business Action Week, the Retail Trust’s Let’s Respect Retail Week, and shopworkers union Usdaw’s Respect for Shopworkers Week.
ShopKind champions will be responsible for sharing the campaign’s message through all communications and will receive a digital ShopKind Champions Pack.
Anyone interested in becoming a ShopKind champion, or looking for more information about ShopKind Week, should email daniel.askew@acs.org.uk.

items.title: How can fashion businesses support buying and merchandising teams?
items.summary: Drapers How can fashion businesses support buying and merchandising teams? items.body:
The wholesaler’s 2027 spring and summer pre-sell platform has been re-designed to be simpler and be clearly visible on mobiles, tablets and desktops, as well as having a wider range of products.

To allow retailers to be more reactive with their price-points, deals have been created across the most-popular branded confectionery lines, while Co-op brand Easter bakery lines are being included in the pre-sell for the first time this year.
Ian King, business development and growth director at Co-op Wholesale, said: “Our brand-new online ordering site is the result of us listening to customers’ feedback.

To mark its introduction into convenience stores, Pepsi is giving retailers the chance to win £1,000 towards a Christmas… This story continues at Pepsi brings new flavour to convenience stores Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Last year the flavour had a limited edition run, but was not available everywhere.
To mark its introduction into convenience stores, Pepsi is giving retailers the chance to win £1,000 towards a Christmas party.
To enter, retailers simply need to pre-order Pepsi zero-sugar gingerbread or Pepsi Max seasonal point of sale materials from Carlsberg Britvic’s At Your Convenience platform and fill out a short form for the chance to win.
As well as the £1,000 top prize, two runners-up will each receive a Pepsi-branded Christmas jumper to keep or give away, alongside a case each of Pepsi zero-sugar gingerbread, Pepsi Max and Pepsi Max cherry, lime and tropical.
David Laidler, brand director of carbonates at Carlsberg Britvic, said: “After the popularity of Pepsi Zero Sugar Gingerbread last year, we knew we had to bring it back even bigger, making it available to more shoppers by expanding into convenience stores.
“We know there is a real demand for new flavours, seasonal treats and affordable indulgence, so its expansion into convenience gives retailers an opportunity to create some festive cheer in-store and encourage shoppers to pick up a can or bottle over the Christmas season.”
Available until the end of December 2026, Pepsi Zero Sugar Gingerbread flavour will roll out across all retail channels in 500ml (RRP £2.15), and eight-can multi-packs (RRP £6.89).
The launch will be supported by a comprehensive marketing campaign spanning shopper, social, digital and PR, alongside in-store activation and sampling.
Alongside the seasonal launch, Pepsi is continuing to strengthen its wider take-home range, with Pepsi Max and Pepsi Max Cherry transitioning into eight-can price-marked multi-packs in time for the festive season.

Founded by Will Best and Harry Farnham, BLOODY was […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
BLOODY Drinks has expanded its supermarket presence with the launch of its flagship BLOODY Bloody Mary into 360 Morrisons stores nationwide.
The new listing gives the brand its broadest grocery distribution to date, adding Morrisons to an existing retail footprint spanning Sainsbury’s, Waitrose, Co-op and Ocado.
Founded by Will Best and Harry Farnham, BLOODY was born from the pair’s frustration at being served disappointing versions of their favourite cocktail. They spent two years developing a Bloody Mary that could deliver the same flavour and consistency every time, with the can keeping the ingredients fresh while making the notoriously fiddly cocktail much easier to serve at home.
At 6.1% ABV, BLOODY Bloody Mary is made with tomato juice and triple-distilled vodka from 58 & Co, with Amontillado, Lea & Perrins Worcestershire Sauce, Kikkoman soy sauce, fresh lemon juice and TABASCO® adding layers of sweetness, umami, acidity and heat.
Its savoury profile gives BLOODY a distinctive position within a canned cocktail category still heavily weighted towards sweeter and fruit-led drinks.
The wider BLOODY range also includes BLOODY Virgin Mary, an alcohol-free cocktail that can also be used as a mixer with a spirit of choice; the aromatic BLOODY Red Snapper, made with The Botanist Gin; and BLOODY Mezcal Maria – a Mexican twist on a Bloody Mary with Ojo de Dios’ artisanal Joven Mezcal.
Will Best, the co-founder of BLOODY Drinks, said: “Getting BLOODY into 360 Morrisons stores is a big moment for us. We started the brand because we love Bloody Marys but were fed up with how difficult it could be to find a really good one.
“Getting BLOODY into 360 Morrisons stores is a big moment for us. We started the brand because we wanted to get our version of this brilliant cocktail to as many people as possible. Morrisons puts BLOODY in front of loads more shoppers across the country and is another big step for the brand as we grow in grocery.”
Matt Brittain, RTD buyer from Morrisons, said: “As the RTD category continues to evolve, our customers are increasingly looking for convenient, bar-quality experiences at home. We are thrilled to welcome Bloody Drinks to our range this September, offering shoppers a bold, premium, and distinctive option
BLOODY Bloody Mary is available at Morrisons, Sainsbury’s, Waitrose, Co-op and Ocado, and online at bloodydrinks.co.uk.

items.title: DRS: the time is now | Editor’s comment
items.summary: There is less than a year to go until the deposit return scheme (DRS) comes into force, yet about three-quarters of retailers responding to a TalkingRetail.com poll remain undecided about how, or whether, they will take part. That uncertainty is understandable. For an independent store,… This story continues at DRS: the time is now | Editor’s comment Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
That uncertainty is understandable. For an independent store, DRS is not simply a matter of putting a machine by the door. It means choosing between manual take-back and a reverse vending machine, training staff, and fitting another task into an already demanding day.
But putting off the decision is no longer an option. Independent retailers will play a fundamental role in whether the scheme succeeds. Exchange for Change has opened registration, and stores need to start working through what DRS will mean for them.
There is no one-size-fits-all answer. A busy forecourt, a city store and a small village shop will face different volumes and costs. Retailers must look closely at their location, customers, space and likely returns before committing themselves.
They should use all the help available. Unitas Wholesale’s free Plan for Profit tools can model return volumes, handling-fee income and storage needs, while symbol groups and the ACS are offering guidance too. It is far better to test the figures now than make an expensive decision in a rush later.
There are strong reasons to take part. Providing a return point is a valuable community service – and serving the community is what good independent retail is all about. It could also bring extra shoppers through the door and, with them, additional sales.
Ireland shows what can be achieved. By March this year, more than 2.5 billion containers had been collected and the proportion recycled had risen from 49% before the scheme to 91%. Its experience also shows that the practical challenges are real and vary sharply between stores.
DRS will take up space and staff time. It will create more work for businesses already under pressure. Those concerns should not be brushed aside. But October 2027 will arrive quickly. The right decision will differ from store to store; the time to start making it is now.
David Shrimpton | Editor

items.title: How to dress a tech oligarch: The Social Reckoning’s costume designer on Zuckerberg’s style evolution
items.summary: Susan Lyall worked with actor Jeremy Strong to research the Meta CEO’s favorite Nikes and luxury sweaters The first Aaron Sorkin Facebook movie, 2010’s The Social Network, helped cement the early aughts image of Mark Zuckerberg rebelling against corporate norms in rumpled hoodies and T-shirts. The follow-up, The Social Reckoning, is carbon-dated from 2019 to 2021. This is “post-hoodie”, as the movie’s costume designer, Susan Lyall, describes it, “post-thumbing his nose” to formality.
