items.title: I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
items.summary: After Primark announced plans for home delivery, we hear from women who never go into clothes stores.
items.body:
I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
- Published
Jess Bacon does all her clothes shopping online.
As a plus-size woman, she finds the size ranges available in stores unreliable. "The sizing in store is notoriously bad. I find it quite demoralising in store," she says.
"The average size woman in the UK is a size 14 or a size 16. I think a lot of people just don't feel seen or represented," says the 29-year-old from Peterborough.
Jess, a culture journalist and author, finds shopping online "much quicker than going into a store, paying for parking, trying things on".
And she feels posting back items that don't fit is less hassle than returning in store, while frequent visits to her local post office give her "more of a community connection".
Jess notes Primark is one of the few High Street retailers where plus-size people can shop. In her experience, Primark stores usually stock up to a size 22.
But soon she'll have the option of staying home even for this - as, after years of holding out, Primark now plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain.
Even throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, when shops were closed, Primark didn't offer the ability to shop online. In 2022 it launched a click-and-collect service, but shoppers still had to travel for their purchases.
The retailer has not said when it expects to launch the service, but has bought a warehouse in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes.
Analysts say the decision shows Primark is facing major challenges from ultra-fast-fashion brands such as Shein.
Online shopping had been on the rise even before the surge seen during the pandemic.
Online accounted for 27.3% of all retail sales in August this year, according to the Office for National Statistics, up from 18.1% in August 2019.
Internet shopping has also been boosted by the decline of the High Street in many parts of the country, something which Jess has noticed in Peterborough. "We don't have John Lewis [anymore]. There's kind of not that much of a reason to go into town."
'I basically never go into clothes shops'
Like Jess, Julia Mitchell, who lives near Chichester, doesn't enjoy in-person clothes shopping. She finds it overstimulating and thinks there are better bargains to be had online.
"I basically never go into them [clothes shops]. It's not really something I enjoy," the 32-year-old says.
"I guess some people might be able to see stuff and pick it up and look at it, but for me, being able to get the best price is more important."
Julia, a content creator, tries to shop ethically and most of her purchases are second hand from Vinted.
The one thing she never shops online for, though, is books. "The thing about bookshops is that they are cultural spaces and community spaces."
Sandra Davies does all her shopping online. She has had three strokes and finds walking to and around stores too much physically.
"I've tried it on two occasions but on both times, standing in a queue for over 10 minutes was too much for me and I collapsed."
The 61-year-old from Sheffield says waiting for deliveries can be taxing as well, as she worries about missing the postie and having to reschedule.
Returns policy can 'make or break'
Julie Palmer, a retail analyst, is not surprised that Primark has finally moved into home deliveries as it has evidently recognised that "online sales bring scale".
However, she says a shop's returns policy for online purchases can "make or break" it. Many brands offer hassle-free returns, which Palmer says Primark must match in order to compete.
"Shoppers want them to be free, simple and quick. That means a generous window, lots of drop-off options and refunds that land within days, not weeks.
"When a policy is clunky or slow, customers remember it and shop elsewhere next time."
But returns are expensive for retailers. Some, like Asos, have started charging a fee if customers make frequent returns.
This is a balancing act, Palmer says, "because a fee can easily push a customer to a competitor".
"Most retailers that charge still offer free returns in store, which is a deliberate way to get people through the door and hopefully spending again."
- My hometown shows that High Streets have to change or die 
  - Published28 September
- Primark finally set to launch home deliveries 
  - Published10 September

British independent fashion and homeware retailer Oliver Bonas is delighted to announce the opening of its brand-new store at Clapham Junction Station on 17 October, bringing its distinctive collection of fashion, homeware, beauty, jewellery and gifts to the UK’s biggest interchange station.
Located within one of London’s busiest rail stations, the new store marks an exciting milestone for Oliver Bonas as it continues to expand its presence across the UK. Designed to make shopping convenient and inspiring for customers on the move, the store offers a carefully curated selection of Oliver Bonas’ latest collections all under one roof.
The opening gives both regular travellers and local shoppers the opportunity to browse womenswear, accessories, jewellery, homeware, beauty and thoughtful gifts. Making it
easy to pick up a last-minute present, refresh their style or discover something new on their daily commute.
Sevda Cankorur, head of retail at Oliver Bonas, said: “Clapham Junction feels like a natural next stop for Oliver Bonas. It’s a brilliant part of London, connecting a busy local community with thousands of people on the move every day. We’re looking forward to bringing our mix of design-led collections to the station, whether customers have time for a browse or are making a quick dash for a last-minute present before their train.”
The new opening further strengthens Oliver Bonas’ presence across London and the wider UK, offering customers another destination to experience the brand’s thoughtful design, joyful product ranges and welcoming in-store experience.

items.body:
Commercial logistics in retail: how efficient shipping drives customer loyalty
In the highly competitive retail and e-commerce landscape, the final leg of the supply chain—the delivery of goods to the end consumer—has become a primary driver of customer satisfaction. A seamless, fast, and transparent shipping experience builds brand loyalty, whereas delayed or damaged packages can permanently damage a retailer’s reputation. Establishing a dependable logistics partnership is therefore a critical business decision for brands operating across the United Kingdom and international markets.
Modern consumers demand complete flexibility and control over how and when their purchases arrive. From real-time tracking maps to dynamic delivery redirection and evening doorstep drop-offs, logistics providers must continuously innovate to meet these elevated expectations. Understanding the mechanics of professional courier services enables retailers and individual senders to optimise shipping workflows, reduce cart abandonment rates, and maintain control over transit costs.
Essential features of an industry-leading delivery partner
Evaluating potential transport providers requires a thorough analysis of their operational infrastructure and digital capabilities across several key areas:
- Guaranteed Delivery Windows: Precise delivery scheduling, including same-day, next-day, and weekend options tailored to consumer preferences.
- Extensive Drop-Off and Pickup Networks: Access to widespread service points, local retail partners, and 24/7 automated lockers for flexible parcel handovers.
- Advanced Tracking and Notifications: Proactive communication tools that keep recipients informed via SMS, email, or mobile app alerts throughout the delivery journey.
- Smooth Returns Management: User-friendly returns procedures that allow customers to easily print return labels or drop off items without hassle.
- Scalable Infrastructure: Ability to handle seasonal volume spikes seamlessly during peak shopping periods without sacrificing transit quality or speed.
- Transparent Cost Structure: Clear, predictable rates based on parcel size and weight, enabling accurate shipping margin planning for retailers.
Cross-border logistics and selecting a reliable shipping Partner
Expanding retail operations beyond national borders requires a partner with specialised international networks. Utilising a professional British parcel service allows businesses to reach European consumers quickly and cost-effectively. Integrated digital customs tools automatically handle required documentation during checkout, reducing border delays and eliminating unexpected customs fees for foreign buyers.
Modern courier networks offer direct transport routes connecting the UK to mainland Europe, providing rapid delivery times that rival domestic transport. Real-time digital tracking systems give senders and recipients full visibility over cross-border shipments, ensuring complete peace of mind and building long-term trust in international e-commerce channels.
Best practices for packaging and protecting commercial goods
Protecting products during automated sorting, stacking, and road transit requires adherence to professional packaging standards. Always use high-quality double-walled corrugated cardboard boxes sized appropriately for the contents. Wrap items individually in protective cushioning, such as bubble wrap or foam, maintaining at least two inches of padding between the contents and the outer walls of the box.
Fill all empty spaces with lightweight cushioning materials to prevent internal movement during handling. Seal all box openings securely using strong, pressure-sensitive packing tape along all seams. Affix the shipping label flatly on the largest surface of the package, ensuring that barcodes and address details are clearly visible and unobstructed by tape, folds, or old shipping marks.

However, growth did decelerate slightly in the second quarter […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Following today’s release of Procook’s figures for the 28 weeks ending 11 October 2026; Emily Scott, retail analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers her view: “ProCook delivered a strong first half for FY2026/27, bolstered by store openings and a robust online proposition. However, growth did decelerate slightly in the second quarter after an exceptional start in Q1, with this early momentum ensuring H1 revenue rose 16.3% to £39.7m. The 13% jump in ProCook’s share price this morning reflects investor confidence in its sustained market outperformance and improving balance sheet, with analysts expecting operating profit of £6.1m for FY2026/27, which would be nearly a 25% uplift on FY2025/26. The retailer enters the second half in a strong position to continue outperforming, with gross margin and operating costs in line with expectations, and inventory built for Black Friday and Christmas success.
“Ecommerce remained the principal growth engine in H1, with revenue up 21.6%, driven by higher traffic and continued investment in its social media and website for a better online experience. ProCook’s focus on customer acquisition and digital engagement through engaging content creation should support further growth in H2, with new customer acquisition up 25% year-on-year, the active customer base up 28%, and attributed revenue from social marketing and content up 46%. The growth in ecommerce strengthens ProCook’s reach and reduces its reliance on store-led growth, while the transition to DHL-operated warehousing and the planned migration to Shopify Plus will support this momentum by strengthening fulfilment capacity and improving the platform for further scale.
“Retail revenue rose 13.5%, driven by store estate expansion. Yet retail like-for-like sales slipped 0.7% in Q2; however, ProCook still achieved modest like-for-like growth of 0.6% for the first half. This dip appears to be temporary rather than a broader slowdown, as the two-year retail like-for-like comparison remained positive at 5.4%. The retailer did note that this weaker result was the impact of hot weather, but Q1, which covered most of the UK heatwaves, did see positive results as shoppers invested in al fresco dining. ProCook opened three stores in H1, alongside two relocations and two refits, ending the period with 80 stores, including 13 in the new format. However, the contribution from new openings is expected to diminish through the rest of the financial year, with ProCook planning fewer store openings in H2 than during the same period last year. The longer-term value of this investment in its stores will depend on repeat purchasing and customer retention, and it must improve how it incentivises repeat visits to maintain momentum. This could be achieved through introducing click & collect, which would increase the number of consumers going into store and encourage impulse purchases.”

What's gone wrong at Poundland and will Britain's 'Del Boy billionaire' ride to the rescue?
items.summary: Chris Dawson, nicknamed Britain's 'Del Boy billionaire' is understood to have joined a number of suitors vying to acquire stricken Poundland, or at least parts of the business.
items.body:
What's gone wrong at Poundland and will Britain's 'Del Boy billionaire' ride to the rescue?
Britain’s ‘Del Boy Billionaire’ has joined the growing number of suitors circling Poundland as the budget retailer fights for survival.
Chris Dawson, 74, who runs CDS Superstores, which owns The Range, Homebase and Wilko, is reportedly considering a deal to buy parts of the business.
He will join the list of interested parties that Poundland’s owners are in talks with, including the retailer’s own employees, to secure a deal ahead of the busy Christmas period.
Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for €1 last year, has struggled to revive the retailer in a prolonged downturn in consumer spending despite its cheaply priced goods.
Chris Dawson, 74, runs CDS Superstores, which owns The Range, Homebase and Wilko
Why has Poundland struggled?
Poundland, which launched in 1990, is battling the damaging impact of higher inflation, which has driven up costs and squeezed margins.
Crucially, shoppers have realised that fewer products in Poundland shops cost £1.
Chains like Poundland have less wriggle room to absorb additional costs or pass on as much of those extra costs to shoppers with constrained budgets.
At the same time, the cost of employing people has increased thanks to Labour's decisions to raise wages and employer National Insurance contributions.
Outside of these external factors, its former owners, the Warsaw-listed Pepco Group, made some wrong moves that have not gone down well with its customers, including putting Pepco clothing in its shops.
Billionaire Chris Dawson, centre, is understood to be one of a range of suitors looking to buy Poundland
Bargain-hunting Poundland customers have also faced higher taxes and rising inflation, which has piled pressure on household budgets. Savvier shoppers are looking to cheaper online alternatives, including Amazon, Temu and TikTok Shop.
Its most recent woes stem back to last year, when it narrowly avoided collapsing into administration. The chain was sold in June 2025 to US firm Gordon Brothers for a nominal €1 amid 'challenging trading conditions'.
By November 2025, around 100 Poundland shops had been shut or earmarked for closure. Two months later, as part of its radical turnaround plan, Poundland had shut 149 stores with 2,200 job losses.
More recently, however, in an update earlier this month, Poundland said it secured like-for-like sales growth in the quarter to September 26, 2026. Its unadjusted fourth quarter like-for-like growth reached 3.3 per cent and 6.4 per cent on an adjusted basis.
Poundland's managing director, Barry Williams, said this month: 'We ended Q4 with significant momentum, returning to positive like-for-like growth and that momentum has only strengthened in the first week of the new financial year.
'Our recovery plan is working, thanks to our investment in simple low pricing and new ranges, powered by our new in-house teams.'
Who wants to buy Poundland now?
Poundland's owner, Gordon Brothers, has put the retailer up for sale, barely more than a year after buying the company from PepCo.
The chain's owner is now in talks with a number of different potential buyers as it seeks a rescue deal, which includes proposals to carve up the business and offers for the entirety of the business.
Billionaire Dawson, owner of The Range, is, according to The Times, understood to be looking to acquire a selection of the discount retailer’s shops.
Dawson got his nickname, the 'Del Boy billionaire', via the press as a reference to his yellow Lamborghini Urus, which has a personalised number plate 'DE11 BOY', a homage to the character Del Boy Trotter from the classic TV show Only Fools and Horses.
Dawson started his career as a market trader, before founding The Range and scaling it to a major high street chain. He has since acquired Wilko and Homebase out of administration.
Supermarket Lidl also hopes to be able to snap up some of its stores if the retailer fails to sell the whole company. The discounter is pushing ahead with a major expansion mission.
Another firm understood to be circling Poundland, or at least some of its shops, is Modella Capital.
The private equity group owns Britain's WH Smith shops, now known as TG Jones stores and previously bought ailing accessories chain Claire's, Hobbycraft and The Original Factory Shop.
All Claire's standalone shops in the UK and Ireland stopped trading earlier this year after its financial woes saw it fall into administration twice in a year.
It has also been reported that Poundland has stressed its preference to sell the business to Irish firm Martin Property Group, which holds real-estate interests spanning shopping centres to hotels.
Martin Property Group recently acquired National Car Parks out of administration.
Poundstretcher owner Fortress Investment Group is also understood to be interested in buying Poundland.
A spokesperson for Poundland told This is Money: 'From a Poundland perspective, our leadership team – including Barry Williams (managing director) - and Andy Bond (Pepco’s former CEO) - have been working with the Martin Property Group on a fully-funded, ready-to-go, solvent offer for the business, keeping it intact and continuing the rapid progress that's already been made.
'While the Martin Property Group is the management team’s preferred partner, their sole intention is to work with whoever can deliver the best result for the business, colleagues, and suppliers to build on the successful recovery that’s already taking shape.'
Gordon Brothers said on Thursday that it had appointed a trio of new board members, Andrew Kirkpatrick, Stephen Welch and Dominic Young to help oversee a sale.
A spokesman said: 'After commencing a thorough sale process for the entirety of the company, prompted by interest from several parties, active discussions continue with a number of potential acquirers. The offers include those from buyers for the whole business and also indicative offers for significant viable parts of the business from established retail operators.
'The Board will now objectively evaluate these options, considering all relevant stakeholders, with a view to minimising uncertainty for the people, suppliers and local communities with an interest in the business and its future.'
Poundland has been put up for sale barely a year after it was purchased by Gordon Brothers
What could a deal mean for Poundland's staff and shoppers?
Union officials at Usdaw, a union representing shopworkers, are understood to have been offered a meeting with Poundland management as they are concerned that owner Gordon Brothers may favour selling Poundland piecemeal.
Bally Auluk, Usdaw’s national officer, has claimed that Poundland is on the verge of falling into administration, putting 12,000 jobs at risk.
Shop closures and job cuts often ensue after a business is acquired, but nothing has been confirmed.
But the business refuted these claims and a spokesman for Poundland said speculation was ‘wide of the mark’.
Jonathan De Mello, founder and chief executive of JDM Retail, told This is Money: 'Poundland’s recent turbulence is a textbook case of strategic over-complication compounded by historic corporate baggage.
'The brand completely lost its way when it strayed from the single price point that defined its core identity, confusing shoppers and adding immense operational complexity by expanding into frozen food, clothing, and a costly e-commerce infrastructure.'
He added: 'As for a potential takeover, the owner of The Range would be an excellent fit. Chris Dawson understands the UK variety discount sector intimately, possesses the supply chain muscle required to make low margins work, and has already demonstrated a clear appetite for estate integration with his acquisition of Wilko.
'A trade buyer of this calibre would bring genuine operational synergy, which is exactly what Poundland needs rather than another round of private equity financial engineering.
'While the ongoing management buyout talks and interest from multiple suitors offer some reassurance for the thousands of employees, staff must brace for further estate rationalisation, as any incoming owner will inevitably need to trim the remaining fat from the store portfolio to secure long-term profitability.'

items.body:
Mr Kipling is set to make Christmas even sweeter in 2026, with four new seasonal launches and a new four-pack format joining its festive range from September. The line-up introduces two Festive Novelty Tarts, two limited-edition Cake Bites tubs and a new, more accessible pack format for Mince Pie Whirls, giving retailers more opportunities to tap into festive occasions across sharing, treating and everyday indulgence.
The cake category at Christmas is worth £307m and reaches 21 million shoppers, but younger consumers remain underrepresented in the category, with under-45 penetration averaging 55% versus 79% among over-45s. With younger shoppers increasingly seeking festive classics with a twist,1 Mr Kipling’s Christmas 2026 range has been developed to bring a more contemporary edge to Christmas through modern flavour combinations, indulgent chocolate experiences, sharing formats and more accessible price points.2
Festive Novelty Tarts bring new energy to Christmas
Mr Kipling is bringing a fresh twist to Christmas with the launch of Chocolate & Gingerbread and White Chocolate & Hazelnut Flavour Festive Novelty Tarts. Inspired by demand for festive classics with a twist, the tarts are the first Mr Kipling range to feature decorative novelty sprinkles, adding extra festive fun and shelf standout. The range leverages flavour territories such as Hazelnut and Chocolate which over-index with younger consumers (under-45s) at 127 and 131 respectively for total cakes. Paired with chocolate to deliver greater indulgence, the range is designed to bring new excitement to familiar festive flavours.3 4
Seasonal Cake Bites expand sharing occasion
The brand is also expanding its festive range with two limited-edition Cake Bites tubs, Gingerbread Cake Bites and Christmassy Cake Bites. Inspired by two of Christmas’ much-loved flavour territories, the range combines the warming taste of gingerbread and the nostalgic flavours of traditional mince pies with a decadent coating of smooth milk chocolate, bringing a more indulgent twist to festive favourites. Available in a bite-sized sharing format, the tubs are designed for festive get-togethers and seasonal indulgence.4
Mince Pie Whirls return in a more accessible four-pack
Completing the line-up is the return of Mr Kipling Mince Pie Whirls, back for Christmas 2026 in a new four-pack format. With Mince Pies now worth more than £75m and remaining one of Christmas’ most-loved flavour territories, the smaller pack size delivers a lower entry price point, helping make the popular festive favourite more accessible while driving trial among younger and lighter seasonal shoppers.5
Naomi Shooman, global marketing director for sweet treats at Premier Foods, said: “Christmas is a crucial time for the category, and mince pies remain at the heart of festive traditions. We know they are a much-loved favourite, but we are always looking for new ways to surprise and delight consumers, from premium treats such as our two-pack Signature Collection Mince Pies to fresh twists on classic festive flavours.
Across the wider range, we’ve introduced new flavour combinations and formats designed to bring fresh excitement to the category, helping retailers appeal to evolving shopper tastes and unlock new seasonal purchase occasions.”
We can already feel the festive spirit in the air, and with Christmas excitement building, there’s no time like the present to get into the festive spirit!”
On top of the two new launches, favourites from Mr Kipling and Cadbury are returning to shelf this year. This includes:
- Mr Kipling Signature Collection All Butter Mince Pies 4
- Mr Kipling Deep Filled Mince Pies
- Mr Kipling Festive Bakewells
- Mr Kipling Frosty Fancies
- Mr Kipling Christmas Slices
- Cadbury Reindeer Cakes
- Cadbury Cake Bars
- Cadbury Mini Yule Logs
- Cadbury Yule Log

items.title: Waitrose launches first gin and vodka made from a UK supermarket’s own crops
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Waitrose has launched Leckford Single Estate Gin and Leckford Single Estate Vodka, the first spirits made from crops grown on a UK supermarket’s own farm. Both spirits are distilled from grain, but it is unusual to know which farm, let alone which field or day it was harvested. These came from a single field at […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Waitrose has launched Leckford Single Estate Gin and Leckford Single Estate Vodka, the first spirits made from crops grown on a UK supermarket’s own farm.
Both spirits are distilled from grain, but it is unusual to know which farm, let alone which field or day it was harvested. These came from a single field at the Waitrose Farm at Leckford in Hampshire, harvested on 10 July, and reached Waitrose shelves just over three months later, in time for Christmas.
The wheat was grown using regenerative practices, which seek to restore the soil, conserve water and support biodiversity. For the spirits, the field grew oilseed rape the year before, was never left bare between harvests, and the seed was sown into narrow strips rather than ploughing the whole field. Both spirits carry Waitrose’s Championing Regenerative Farming logo, which also appears on Waitrose’s own-label milk and shows products from farms using these practices.
It is the first time the estate has grown a crop specifically for spirits. Leckford wheat has gone into Leckford Homebaking flour since 2003 and Leckford bread since 2024, but this year the Leckford team grew three new varieties as a bespoke spirit grain, chosen with Ramsbury, the Wiltshire estate distillery that made the gin and vodka.
Leckford is where Waitrose has farmed to regenerative principles since 2020. It works closely with farmers and growers, supporting Waitrose Farming for Nature programme, a commitment for all its UK farmers and growers to have started using regenerative practices by 2030.
Regenerative farming also depends on farmers being able to sell what they grow. When it launched Farming for Nature in 2024, Waitrose committed to providing a market for regeneratively produced food, and the spirits give Leckford’s wheat a new one. They take the Leckford range to 17 products, alongside the estate’s bread, flour, oil and honey for food lovers who want to know exactly where their food comes from.
The spirits are the latest in a line of firsts from Leckford. Vines planted there in 2009 made Waitrose the first UK retailer with its own vineyard and the first supermarket to sell its own English sparkling wine. In 2023 it became the first UK retailer to run tractors on renewable natural gas. And in 2024 Leckford’s vineyard and orchards became the first in the UK to gain Regenified certification, an independent standard for regenerative farming.
The wheat is distilled in small batches at Ramsbury, which runs on renewable energy. The gin takes its inspiration from the wild plants that grow across the estate. Its 11 botanicals include juniper, sweet orange, lemon and warming cinnamon. The vodka is distilled four times for a smooth texture with notes of caramel and vanilla. The harvest made 30,000 bottles, on sale now in over 200 Waitrose shops at £25 each.
Andrew Hoad, director of the Leckford Estate and Farming for Nature at Waitrose, said: “We’ve grown wheat for baking at Leckford for more than twenty years, but this is the first time we’ve grown it for spirits. Our commitment to regenerative farming reflects the belief that producing high-quality food and caring for the environment go hand in hand, and these spirits are a taste of exactly that.”
Nik Fordham, Master Distiller and general manager at Ramsbury, said: “Distilling grain grown on a single farm gives us an incredible level of connection to the raw material and the land it comes from. Working with the team at Leckford, we were able to select wheat varieties specifically for their suitability for distilling, considering how their characteristics would influence the flavour, texture and quality of the finished spirits. The choice of grain is fundamental to what we make, and being involved from the field through to distillation allows us to understand and celebrate that journey. It’s a great example of what can be achieved when farming and distilling expertise come together, creating spirits with a genuine sense of place and a clear connection to the land.”

items.title: Fix 'broken' business rates system once and for all, Chancellor told in letter from 200 bosses
items.summary: More than 200 employers have called on the Chancellor to tear up the 'broken' business rates system to revive Britain's battered high streets.
items.body:
Fix 'broken' business rates system once and for all, Chancellor told in letter from 200 bosses
More than 200 employers have called on the Chancellor to tear up the 'broken' business rates system to revive Britain's battered high streets.
In a letter to John Healey ahead of the Budget, the business leaders warn the levy is holding back investment, jobs and growth by placing a 'disproportionate burden' on physical stores.
They argue that 'piecemeal' changes – such as support for pubs proposed by Andy Burnham – have created an increasingly complicated system that 'picks winners and losers without ever fixing the underlying problem'.
The letter – whose signatories range from hotelier Sir Rocco Forte and the bosses of Boodles and The Ritz to galleries and the owners of nurseries and cafes – calls on the government to adopt a new 'hybrid' model involving a 2 per cent levy on online sales and a 37 per cent cut for bricks-and-mortar firms.
Forte, chairman of Rocco Forte Hotels, said: 'Hotels are facing average business rates increases of 115 per cent over the next three years, a level that will be unsustainable for some and will inevitably kill investment and jobs.
'We need fundamental reform, not another round of piecemeal reliefs for a few sectors. The hybrid business rate offers a practical way to create a fairer system which ensures online businesses make their contribution and reduces the burden on businesses that invest in physical premises.'
New Chancellor John Healey has been urged to fix the 'broken' business rates system following the botched reforms of his predecessor Rachel Reeves
Sir Rocco Forte is among the business leaders calling for reform
Michael Wainwright, managing director of Boodles, a family-owned jeweller for six generations, said: 'Businesses that invest in bricks and mortar, employ people and contribute to the life of our high streets should not carry a disproportionate share of the tax burden simply because they have physical premises.
'At Boodles, our stores are an important part of how we engage with customers and showcase British design and craftsmanship, but the cost of occupying those premises is a significant fixed cost.'
The intervention – less than two weeks ahead of the Budget on October 28 – underlines the anger among business chiefs over Rachel Reeves' botched reforms of the rates system.
Having pledged to level the playing field between the high street and online rivals, the former Chancellor hammered business with a spiralling rates bill.
Business leaders are now calling on Burnham and Healey to act – though it is feared the Chancellor will instead announce support for the high street rather than fundamental reform.
The letter, which was organised by the Real Rates Reform Alliance and brings together senior figures from retail and hospitality to tourism, property and leisure, said: 'We welcomed the recent announcement by the Prime Minister to cut business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues.
'However, while this decision recognises some of the inadequacies within the current business rates system, it is not the fundamental change required to fix this broken system once and for all.
'We believe this moment now presents a unique opportunity to go further and create a business tax system that fixes the current regime's fundamental imbalances, supports firms across all sectors and drives investment in communities and long-term economic growth.'
It concludes: 'Britain has spent three decades adjusting business rates instead of resolving their fundamental flaws. The time has come to modernise this broken system.
'We call on you to seize this opportunity to create a business tax system that is simpler, fairer, more sustainable, and better aligned with the economy of the future.'
Ros Morgan, chairman of the Real Rates Reform Alliance, said: 'This letter shows that business rates reform is a concern across every sector of business and right across the UK. Businesses recognise that the current system is holding back investment, growth and jobs.
'Decades of piecemeal reliefs have failed to fix the underlying problem. The Government now has an opportunity to deliver fundamental reform rather than simply move the burden between sectors.
'The hybrid business rate would cut the burden on businesses investing in physical places while broadening the tax base. With the Budget approaching, the Chancellor should seize this opportunity to deliver lasting reform.'
Boodles managing director Michael Wainwright, whose jewellery has been modelled by Lady Amelia and Lady Eliza Spencer
Helen Swaby, chief executive of Clarendon Fine Art, said: 'With more than 90 galleries, our physical presence is at the heart of what we do. Business rates are therefore a significant and unavoidable cost.
'We need a system that recognises the value bricks-and-mortar businesses bring to our high streets and town centres, rather than placing a disproportionate burden on those that invest in them.
'If we want thriving town centres and successful businesses across the country, we need a rates system that supports investment in physical places as part of thriving communities.'
Anda Rowland, director of Anderson & Sheppard, tailors to the King, said: 'Business rates are not an abstract tax for a business like ours.
'We employ highly skilled people and invest in training the next generation of craftspeople, but every increase in the cost of our premises puts greater pressure on our ability to invest in those people and in the future of the business.
'We need a business rates system that recognises the value created by businesses that invest in people, skills and physical places.'
The letter sent to the Chancellor
Dear Chancellor,
Across the UK, too many towns and cities are being held back from realising their economic potential.
In 2024 alone, almost 13,000 shops closed (around 37 every day), as rising costs continued to outpace growth.
Businesses that invest in communities create jobs, drive productivity and sustain local economies, yet the current business rates system places a disproportionate burden on those businesses, while an increasing share of economic activity now takes place online without making a proportional contribution to the tax base.
Against this backdrop, we welcomed the recent announcement by the Prime Minister to cut business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues.
However, while this decision recognises some of the inadequacies within the current business rates system, it is not the fundamental change required to fix this broken system once and for all.
We believe this moment now presents a unique opportunity to go further and create a business tax system that fixes the current regime's fundamental imbalances, support firms across all sectors and drive investment in communities and long-term economic growth.
For more than two decades, governments of all colours have sought to reform business rates through new reliefs, exemptions and differential multipliers for individual sectors.
While often well-intentioned, this piecemeal approach has produced an excessively complex set of reliefs and special provisions that picks winners and losers without ever fixing the underlying problem.
The result is a fundamentally flawed system that is harder to understand, less economically rational and increasingly disconnected from the way the modern economy operates.
The next phase of business rates reform should build upon sector-specific interventions and modernise the system itself. The tax system should better reflect where economic activity takes place.
We therefore urge you to consider a fundamental reset, of the sort Labour promised in opposition.
We believe the Hybrid Business Rate is the comprehensive reform that this moment requires.
It combines a lower property-based business rate with a modest levy on eligible online sales across the economy.
The levy would be collected through the existing tax system, using an established administrative mechanism that minimises additional costs for businesses and government.
Broadening the tax base in this way would generate sufficient revenue to reduce business rates by up to 37 per cent, while maintaining sustainable funding for local government.
Carefully designed exemptions would ensure that the levy applies only to eligible online sales, protects small businesses and continues to support investment in physical places and experiences.
A Hybrid Business Rate is more than a reform of business rates. It is a modern fiscal framework designed for today's economy, one that supports investment and provides combined authorities with a broader and more resilient tax base to underpin devolution, infrastructure, and long-term place-based growth.
Britain has spent three decades adjusting business rates instead of resolving their fundamental flaws. The time has come to modernise this broken system.
We call on you to seize this opportunity to create a business tax system that is simpler, fairer, more sustainable, and better aligned with the economy of the future.

items.title: Healey’s £1bn London office raid would be ‘attack on growth’
items.summary: John Healey’s potential £1bn raid on London offices would be an “attack on growth” and deal a huge blow to the City, property firms have warned.  The Chancellor is weighing up an increase to business rates for expensive office blocks and skyscrapers which would raise £1bn for the Treasury but disproportionately hit the capital’s business [...]
items.body:
Healey’s £1bn London office raid would be ‘attack on growth’
John Healey’s potential £1bn raid on London offices would be an “attack on growth” and deal a huge blow to the City, property firms have warned.
The Chancellor is weighing up an increase to business rates for expensive office blocks and skyscrapers which would raise £1bn for the Treasury but disproportionately hit the capital’s business districts, the Telegraph has reported.
The tax raid threat will raise alarm bells for the City, with bank bosses already fearing Healey could launch an assault on their profits.
The policy would result in “less investment, fewer jobs and lower tax revenues for the whole country,” said the boss of the City Property Association, which represents more than 100 major property developers.
The plans being reviewed by the Chancellor would hike business rates for commercial buildings with a value higher than £500,000.
The Treasury would exclude the high street from the tax hike by exempting larger retail and hospitality premises from the increase in rates.
The measure would affect some 9,000 properties in London and the South East, according to tax firm Ryan, with Canary Wharf and the Square Mile being heavily affected.
Vanessa Hale, chief executive of trade body Real Estate UK, said the government cannot “tax its way to delivering good growth in every postcode” – the key pledge set out by Healey and Andy Burnham ahead of this month’s Budget.
She said: “House builders are already pulling out of the capital and it seems the government doesn’t care if commercial property developers do too. This isn’t a good growth policy – it’s an attack on growth policy and simply masks the failure to get on and fully reform the business rates system properly.”
Office tax would ‘undermine investment’
CPA chair Nikki Dibley said: “Increasing the cost of occupying office space to the very businesses that are the engines of our economy risks weakening the UK’s competitiveness at exactly the moment we should be making it easier, not harder, for them to locate here and grow.
“The result is likely to be less investment, fewer jobs and lower tax revenues for the whole country,” she said.
A London business association said any measure to deter major businesses from setting up their headquarters in the capital would damage the UK’s global reputation.
John Dickie, chief executive of BusinessLDN, said: “London competes globally to attract major businesses and corporate headquarters so hiking taxes on large office buildings risks undermining the UK’s ability to attract international investment.
“Rather than making piecemeal changes, the Government should deliver on its manifesto commitment to replace the business rates system in a way that encourages investment and drives growth.”
A Treasury spokesperson said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the Chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

items.title: Lidl eyes Poundland bargain as sale of discount retailer ramps up
items.summary: Discount supermarket Lidl has tabled a bid for a single Poundland shop in the hope of scooping up more stores if the retailer is broken up, City AM has learned. The German grocery chain has put in an offer to Gordon Brothers, which owns the retailer, in which it would initially buy one store if [...]
items.body:
Lidl eyes Poundland bargain as sale of discount retailer ramps up
Discount supermarket Lidl has tabled a bid for a single Poundland shop in the hope of scooping up more stores if the retailer is broken up, City AM has learned.
The German grocery chain has put in an offer to Gordon Brothers, which owns the retailer, in which it would initially buy one store if the company’s sale process fails and it is broken up, City AM understands.
Lidl’s bid would then allow it “cherry pick” a further small number of Poundland stores if the company ended up being split up between a number of individual buyers, according to sources close to the sale process.
The German discounter is one of a number of retailers who are vying for a break-up of Poundland. Between six and eight retailers have put in bids for some of its stores, the sources said.
It had been reported that Aldi, Lidl’s rival, was considering putting in a bid but City AM understands it is not in talks with Gordon Brothers.
Lidl’s involvement in Poundland’s sale comes as the discount supermarket plans to open more than 50 stores in the next year. The grocer has been growing its market share as rival UK supermarkets see their presence in the sector stall.
While Lidl and others have only proposed to buy a specific number of Poundland’s sites, other bidders are proposing to buy hundreds of its shops.
The owner of The Range and Wilko is among the retail heavyweights battling for control of the discount retailer, The Times has reported. Chris Dawson’s CDS Superstores had been weighing a bid for the entirety of Poundland but is now only interested in parts of the business and a limited number of its locations.
Beyond the retailers hoping to snap up extra sites from Poundland’s sale, a number of investment groups have tabled bids for the business.
Directors parachuted in as sale speeds up
Poundland’s management have expressed preference for a bid tabled by Martin Property Group (MPG), the Irish firm which recently bought National Car Parks (NCP).
The discount retailer has parachuted in three independent directors to join its board, Sky News first reported. These new members are Andrew Kirkpatrick, Stephen Welch and Dominic Young.
These directors have been added to the board to address concerns among MPG’s rival bidders that its two existing members, Barry Williams and Shaun Wills, have publicly expressed support for one of the proposals.
The presence of additional experts on Poundland’s board is intended to offer reassurance to bidders that their proposals will be considered fairly.
A spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said: “After commencing a thorough sale process for the entirety of the company, prompted by interest from several parties, active discussions continue with a number of potential acquirers.
“The offers include those from buyers for the whole business and also indicative offers for significant viable parts of the business from established retail operators.
“The Board will now objectively evaluate these options, considering all relevant stakeholders, with a view to minimising uncertainty for the people, suppliers and local communities with an interest in the business and its future.”
Gordon Brothers kicked off its sale of Poundland last month, little more than a year after buying the company for a nominal £1 fee from retail group PepCo.
Advisors Alvarez & Marsal, who were appointed to run the sale, are weighing up bids from a number of buyers. These include proposals to carve up the business and offers for the entirety of the company.
Poundstretcher owner Fortress Investment Group and TG Jones owner Modella Capital are among the other parties who have expressed an interest in Poundland.
Poundland and Lidl were contacted for comment. Alvarez & Marsal declined to comment.

items.title: The Retail Trust partners with SAI, strengthening its safer stores mission
items.summary: The Retail Trust has teamed up with Storewide Active Intelligence (SAI), which has become an official partner of the charity as part of SAI’s work to support retail workers’ safety and wellbeing. Already working with major grocers, including the Big Four, Iceland and Our Coop,… This story continues at The Retail Trust partners with SAI, strengthening its safer stores mission Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Already working with major grocers, including the Big Four, Iceland and Our Coop, as well as leading fashion brands, SAI’s solution unifies Loss Prevention (LP) and insight-led store operations.
Using its patented Visual Language Model (VLM), the SAI One platform blends computer vision with GenAI to turn traditionally ‘passive’ store surveillance systems into an active, operational platform for real-time store intelligence.
As part of its work with leading brands on LP, SAI helps retailers reduce in-store violence, colleague abuse and shrink via its facial recognition technology (FRT) solution.
Born out of its founding principle that stores should be safe, community spaces free from crime and violence, SAI redistributes earnings from its violence prevention and FRT systems, setting them aside as a charitable trust.
It then uses these funds to support causes and charities that champion store safety, spanning colleague protection and wellbeing, rehabilitation projects supporting those with addictions who turn to shoplifting, and wider work with the policing and justice communities.
“When we launched SAI, we knew we never wanted to profit from violence – we’d rather there was no need for this technology at all,” Helen Wilde, co-founder & chief commercial officer at SAI, explained.
“But with more and more retailers coming to us and needing our solution to tackle the problem, we decided to ensure revenues generated from this part of the business were used to do good and give back.”
In addition to supporting the charity, SAI will develop new ways to use intelligence help tackle repeat offenders.
With the top 10% of repeat retail offenders estimated to be responsible for between 68 – 70% of total in-store retail crime, its efforts will help reduce retail loss while making stores safer spaces for colleagues and communities.
Chris Brook-Carter, chief executive of the Retail Trust, said: “We are grateful for SAI’s support as we explore new ways of protecting retail workers against abuse, violence and theft and the impact this can have on their wellbeing.
“Our partnership will build on the help the Retail Trust is already providing to hundreds of retailers and people working across the industry to create happier and safer retail workplaces.”
Wilde added: “We’ve long admired the work the Retail Trust does – both through the practical support it delivers to retail workers and by championing colleague wellbeing through awareness campaigns.”
“This made partnering with them a natural step as we further our commitment to creating safer retail environments that support colleagues, customers and communities.”
The partnership with the Retail Trust comes as SAI prepares to launch its new Safer Stores initiative, which brings together diverse stakeholders – from major retailers to crime and justice bodies, rehabilitation groups and technology providers – in a shared mission to improve the safety of bricks-and-mortar environments.
Meanwhile, hundreds of businesses will back the Retail Trust’s Let’s Respect Retail campaign this Christmas by increasing employee support and calling for more respect from shoppers.

items.title: DRESSX launches 360° AI commerce analytics to track the customer journey from question to purchase
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. A growing part of online shopping is beginning to happen before a customer ever reaches a retailer’s website. Consumers can now ask AI what to buy, describe exactly what they need, compare products and brands, and narrow down their choices within a conversation. For brands, much of that new customer journey is difficult to see. […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
A growing part of online shopping is beginning to happen before a customer ever reaches a retailer’s website. Consumers can now ask AI what to buy, describe exactly what they need, compare products and brands, and narrow down their choices within a conversation.
For brands, much of that new customer journey is difficult to see.
DRESSX is launching a new suite of AI commerce analytics tools designed to change that, giving brands a 360° view of how consumers discover and engage with products through AI – from the questions they ask and the recommendations they receive to the traffic, carts and purchases that follow.
The launch comes as AI visibility is quickly becoming a new priority for brands and retailers, as they look to understand how they appear across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and other AI platforms. DRESSX is taking that conversation further, connecting AI visibility with actual ecommerce performance.
“AI is changing not only where people discover products, but how they make decisions,” said Daria Shapovalova and Natalia Modenova, co-founders of DRESSX. “A customer can now have an entire conversation about what to buy before ever reaching a brand’s website. For brands, that creates a new part of the customer journey they need to understand and measure. We’ve learned how to measure search and social. Now we need to understand AI in the same way.”
The new suite brings together two proprietary tools designed to give brands visibility into different parts of that journey.
AI Visibility shows brands what consumers see when they ask AI what to buy. It tracks relevant questions across AI platforms, revealing which brands and products are recommended, where competitors appear instead, and which sources are shaping AI responses.
AI Revenue Tracker connects AI discovery with ecommerce performance, showing which AI platforms are sending traffic to a brand’s website and how those visitors progress from sessions to carts and completed orders.
Together, the tools connect discovery, visibility and conversion, helping brands understand what consumers are looking for, what AI is showing them, where their brand sits within those recommendations, and what happens when AI discovery turns into a website visit. DRESSX CTO Ivan Zaparovannyi led the product from initial concept through development and implementation:
“For a growing number of consumers, AI is starting to replace the Google search they would have used to decide what to buy,” said Ivan Zaparovannyi, CTO of DRESSX. “The answer is the new shelf. It decides which brands get discovered, which ones get recommended, and which ones never enter the customer journey at all. That is the shift every brand needs to understand.”
The launch expands DRESSX’s work in AI-powered ecommerce beyond customer-facing technologies including Virtual Try-On and AI styling into the analytics behind the customer journey.
As AI becomes another gateway to online shopping, DRESSX expects AI commerce analytics to become a standard part of the ecommerce stack, alongside search, social and website analytics.
The new AI commerce analytics suite is available through More Dash Ads.

items.title: GMFRS prosecutes fireworks distributor and two retailers over licensing breaches
items.summary: A national fireworks distributor and two Greater Manchester shopkeepers have been prosecuted following investigations into breaches of explosives legislation by the Greater Manchester Fire Rescue Service (GMFRS). At Manchester Magistrates' Court on 6 October, Hashum Malik, director of Boom Fireworks, pleaded guilty to offences relating… This story continues at GMFRS prosecutes fireworks distributor and two retailers over licensing breaches Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
At Manchester Magistrates’ Court on 6 October, Hashum Malik, director of Boom Fireworks, pleaded guilty to offences relating to the storage of fireworks after specialist GMFRS inspectors discovered around 200kg of Hazard Type 3 (HT3) fireworks being stored contrary to licensing requirements.
In separate cases heard at Tameside Magistrates Court on 11 September, Shabaz Ali Abbas, of Broomhurst Avenue, Oldham, and Said Shiragha Hashimi, of Nevada Street, Manchester, were sentenced for offences under the Explosives Regulations 2014.
The prosecutions were brought by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) which licenses the storage of explosives, including fireworks, across the city-region.
The court heard that Boom Fireworks Limited, which operates distribution premises in Cheetham Hill and Rochdale, was found to be storing approximately 200kg of HT3 fireworks in breach of explosives legislation.
HT3 fireworks present a greater fire, blast and projectile risk than standard HT4 retail fireworks and are therefore subject to stricter storage requirements.
Following a GMFRS inspection, the fireworks were detained and removed from the premises.
Boom Fireworks Limited was fined £40,000, and a £2,000 surcharge. The court also awarded full prosecution costs of £3,482.16, making the total fine £45,485.16.
In Oldham, Abbas was found to be storing and selling fireworks at The Vape Store on Hollins Road, Oldham, he owns, despite his explosives licence having expired on 31 October 2024.
When specialist fire safety inspectors visited the premises on 2 November 2024, they found fireworks still being stored, including higher-risk Hazard Type 3 (HT3) fireworks.
The stock was detained and removed. Abbas was sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, and ordered to complete a 10-day community order.
The court also awarded full prosecution costs of £4,162.11, together with a victim surcharge of £187. The fireworks seized from the premises were also ordered to be destroyed.
In Bolton, inspectors found fireworks being stored and sold at Wise Buys on Bury Road, Bolton, without a valid explosives licence.
Owner, Hashimi had taken over the business in 2023 but had not applied for a licence in his own name.
Inspectors found fireworks stored in unsuitable conditions, including some HT3 fireworks at premises with residential accommodation above.
Hashimi was sentenced to 25 days of Rehabilitation Activity Requirement, requiring him to participate in targeted rehabilitative programmes.
He was also made subject to a three-month curfew. The court awarded full prosecution costs of £4,281.82 and a victim surcharge of £114.
The fireworks seized from the premises were also ordered to be destroyed.
Kate Green, deputy mayor for safer and stronger communities, said: “Fireworks are enjoyed by many people across Greater Manchester at this time of year. Storing them safely is essential to protecting the public, businesses and property.
“These prosecutions demonstrate that we will take robust action against anyone who fails to store, supply or sell fireworks safely and legally.
“We are committed to supporting businesses that want to comply with the law, but we will not hesitate to take tough enforcement action against those who put our communities and firefighters at risk.”
Karl Gibbons, head of protection at Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service, said: “Fireworks are explosives and the rules governing how they are stored exist to protect businesses, residents, customers and the wider public.
“These prosecutions involve both a national distributor and local retailers, but the message is the same regardless of the size of the business. Anyone storing fireworks must understand and comply with their legal responsibilities.
“Our inspectors work closely with businesses throughout the year to help them meet those requirements and maintain safe storage arrangements.
“However, when businesses fail to comply with the law and create unnecessary risk, we will not hesitate to take enforcement action, including prosecution.”
With the main fireworks sales period approaching on 15 October, GMFRS is reminding businesses that anyone storing, supplying or selling fireworks must ensure they have the appropriate licences in place and are complying with explosives legislation.
Failure to do so may result in enforcement action, including prosecutions.
Further guidance on licensing requirements, storage standards and explosives legislation is available here.

items.title: ClearBank CEO: If there’s a fire, run towards it
items.summary: Mark Fairless, CEO at ClearBank Group, takes us through his career, from Tesco to fintech, in today's Square Mile and Me.
items.body:
ClearBank CEO: If there’s a fire, run towards it
We dig into the memory bank of the City’s great and good. Today, Mark Fairless, CEO at ClearBank Group, takes us through his career, from Tesco to fintech, in Square Mile and Me
CV
- Name: Mark Fairless
- Job title: CEO at ClearBank Group
- Previous roles: CFO at ClearBank; heritage CFO at M&G; earlier roles at Santander and Barclays Capital
- Age: 42
- Born: Milton Keynes
- Lives: Surrey
- Studied: History at Bristol, Accounting at Kaplan Financial
- Talents: Dad jokes and karaoke – Blur’s Park Life is my go-to.
- Motto: There’s only two people you need to impress: your eight-year-old self, and your 80-year-old self
- Biggest perk of the job? The people I get to meet. Through our clients and my involvement in the wider fintech industry, I get to engage with some really interesting and influential people. I also love having a voice in the industry and the opportunity to help shape positive change.
- Coffee order: White Americano. I’m also a big fan of Pret coffee – I’m aware that might be an unpopular opinion
- Cocktail order: Red wine, thanks. I’ll happily skip the cocktails.
- Favourite book: Never Split the Difference – Chris Voss. A fascinating read which flips traditional negotiation on its head.
What was your first job?
On the checkout at Tesco in Milton Keynes. I was pretty quick with the scanner and regularly got asked if I was paid by the beep.
What was your first role in the City?
I started out as a graduate accountant at PwC in audit. I worked with a real mix of businesses, from oil companies to nightclubs. My final placement was at Lehman Brothers, and I remember being one of the few people walking into the building while everyone else seemed to be walking out with cardboard boxes. It was surreal.
When did you know you wanted to build a career in the City?
I actually wanted to be a doctor, but some work experience quickly made me realise it wasn’t the career for me. I studied history instead, and when I graduated in the early 2000s, the City was where all the energy seemed to be. In many ways, it was the fintech sector of its day, and I wanted to be part of that.
What’s one thing you love about the City of London?
I love the mix of old and new. One minute you’re walking past St Paul’s and all that history, the next you’re looking up at a brand new building.
And one thing you would change?
I’m not sure it’s about changing something, but about making sure we don’t stand still. The UK has a fantastic position as a global financial centre, but maintaining that means embracing change, continuing to innovate and creating the right environment for businesses to grow.
What’s been your most memorable business lunch or meeting?
It would have to be Davos this year, where I joined the UK delegation with Rachel Reeves. The opportunity to be in the room with world leaders and some fascinating people made it an experience I won’t forget.
And any business faux pas?
I once found myself at a dinner with a very well-known US political figure who I completely failed to recognise. I asked him his name. He wasn’t impressed.
What’s been your proudest moment?
Becoming CEO at 41. Seeing ClearBank grow from a fintech challenger into an established part of the UK’s financial infrastructure has been hugely rewarding. Today, we support more than 300 clients across financial services and the corporate world, have built a profitable UK business and established ourselves in Europe, with plenty more still to do.
And who do you look up to?
My dad. He worked incredibly hard and always encouraged me to make the most of every opportunity. Thanks to him, my brother and I were the first in our family to go to university. He taught me the value of hard work, but also the importance of being fair and treating people well.
What’s the best career advice you’ve ever been given?
If there’s a fire, run towards it rather than away from it. In other words, don’t shy away from difficult problems. And trust your instincts: keep doing what you think is right until someone tells you to stop.
And the worst?
Bang your fists on the table more to get your own way. I’ve always found there are better ways to bring people with you.
Are you optimistic for the year ahead?
Yes, always. I’d much rather be optimistic about what’s ahead and risk the odd disappointment than not take the chance at all.
We’re going for lunch, and you’re picking – where are we going?
I love a good steak, so I’d go for Gaucho in Broadgate Circus. It also happens to be right next to our new office, which is very convenient.
And if we’re grabbing a drink after work?
Any pub on Watling Street. There’s always a great atmosphere after work, you can’t really go wrong.
Where’s home during the week?
You’ll mostly find me at ClearBank’s offices in Broadgate Tower. We’re on the 27th floor, with some pretty impressive views across London.
And where might we find you at the weekend?
Usually out walking my dog, Maverick, or ferrying my children around. My weekends involve quite a lot of unpaid taxi driving.
You’ve got a well-deserved two weeks off. Where are you going and who with?
With two young children, adventure holidays are off the agenda for now. Give me a five-star, all-inclusive resort, a beach and my family, and I’m very happy.

items.title: Dunelm well-positioned for growth after being hampered by heatwaves, says GlobalData
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Following today’s release of Dunelm’s figures for the 13 weeks ending 26 September 2026; Oliver Maddison, senior retail analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers his view: “Dunelm appeared to put in a slightly anaemic performance in its Q1, with sales growing just 1.1%; looking beneath the surface reveals a more encouraging […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Following today’s release of Dunelm’s figures for the 13 weeks ending 26 September 2026; Oliver Maddison, senior retail analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers his view: “Dunelm appeared to put in a slightly anaemic performance in its Q1, with sales growing just 1.1%; looking beneath the surface reveals a more encouraging picture. The first six weeks of the period saw an approximately 3% decline as instore trading was hampered by heatwaves, whereas the final seven weeks, which were cooler, saw sales growth of approximately 4% as consumers felt more comfortable venturing out. Additionally, Dunelm’s Q1 last year was a particularly strong comparative, unhampered by dented consumer confidence from the Iran war or by such an excessively hot summer. Although some of that c.4% rebound in the final seven weeks was a release of pent-up demand from the prior six, investors took heart at the upward trend as well as the 0.1ppt increase in gross margins from favourable foreign-exchange rates, with Dunelm’s share price jumping c.6% in early-morning trading.
“Dunelm’s continued range rationalisation is helping to boost sales and margins as it emphasises ranges consumers want to buy, with plain-dye bedding and cook and dine being the primary beneficiaries. Made-to-measure proved especially strong, achieving double-digit growth. Here, Dunelm attributed growth to a strong execution from its store colleagues, reflecting that despite increasing digital penetration across the business, stores and in-person customer service have an important place in a home specialist’s arsenal. In its refreshing and reallocating of store space, Dunelm should focus on categories which benefit most from strong instore customer service, such as made-to-measure window dressings.
“While store-enabled l-f-l sales declined by 0.8%, reflecting suppressed footfall during the heatwaves, ongoing store refits (four were completed during Q1) will push that figure upwards, while total store-only sales will be buoyed by store openings, with two planned for Q2. These store refits and improved product availability through the rollout of RFID will increase customer engagement with stores, but the homewares market leader would do well to future-proof these refits against heatwaves by ensuring they are air-conditioned. Dunelm’s ever increasing online capacity will partially insulate the retailer from the impacts of future heatwaves, giving consumers an alternative to shopping instore, but air-conditioned stores will attract consumers looking to escape the heat in summers to come.”

items.title: THG raises full year profit expectations as Nutrition offsets a weaker quarter for Beauty, says GlobalData

Following today’s release of THG’s figures for the quarter ending 30 September 2026; Charlotte Chilcott, retail analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers her view: “THG has continued to strengthen its profitability in Q3 FY2026, despite a slowdown in revenue growth, with full-year adjusted EBITDA expectations lifted to £103m. This was driven […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Following today’s release of THG’s figures for the quarter ending 30 September 2026; Charlotte Chilcott, retail analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers her view: “THG has continued to strengthen its profitability in Q3 FY2026, despite a slowdown in revenue growth, with full-year adjusted EBITDA expectations lifted to £103m. This was driven by improving profits in the group’s Nutrition division, supported by a 20% decline in whey prices since the interim results on 10 September 2026. Forecast free cash flow of £25m to £35m would be THG’s first positive year since public listing in 2020, an important step in rebuilding investor confidence. Shares rose 17% in early morning trading as the update eased concerns raised at the H1 results.
“THG Nutrition grew 5.3% in Q3, a slowdown from 9.2% in H1 but a solid result against a tough comparative of 10.0% growth in Q3 2025. New licensing partnerships with Krispy Kreme, Caffè Nero and Iceland built on existing tie-ups such as Mars and Müller, deepening Myprotein’s presence in everyday food occasions and increasing its visibility with mainstream shoppers in grocery and food-to-go channels. The UK launch of Myprotein Rewards will encourage repeat purchasing in a category where shoppers readily switch brands on price, while giving THG richer customer data that can be used to personalise offers, target promotions more efficiently and inform product development. Easing whey prices, together with long-term contracts for other key ingredients such as creatine, collagen and vegan proteins, give the division greater cost certainty into Q4 and FY2027. This should allow Myprotein to protect margins while keeping its pricing competitive, which is increasingly important as mainstream food brands move into protein with their own high-protein ranges.
“THG Beauty revenue fell 0.6% in Q3, a reversal after 5.9% growth in H1, impacted by EU duty and tariff changes and the deferred timing of a large customer contract. The contract revenue has been deferred rather than lost, so should benefit future quarters, but the tariff impact is more persistent, with initiatives for mitigation not due to be complete until Q2 2027, leaving margins under pressure for several more months. Revenue growth is expected to accelerate in Q4, supported by the Advent and gifting season, which is a key trading period for THG Beauty. The Lookfantastic Fragrance Advent Calendar selling out in a day highlights strong demand for the format, which remains an important revenue and profit contributor through Q4. Lookfantastic’s move onto the YouTube Shopping Affiliate Programme adds a new sales channel and builds on its TikTok Shop success, allowing it to reach consumers through creator-led content, which carry particular influence in beauty.”

items.body:
Biomel is expanding its award-winning Prebiotic Gut Health Bar range with the launch of two new flavours – Peanut Butter and Apple & Cinnamon.
The two new variants join Biomel’s existing Belgian Chocolate, Chocolate Hazelnut, Red Berry and Chocolate Orange bars – taking the range to six flavours. Peanut Butter combines a rich, creamy peanut flavour with a subtle hint of salt, while Apple & Cinnamon features juicy apple pieces with cinnamon for a warm, gently spiced flavour. Both are available to purchase from Biomel’s website, with an RRP of £24 per pack of 12 (£2 per bar).
Each 45g bar contains 13g of fibre – around 40% of the recommended daily intake – including a blend of prebiotic fibre and 7 different whole grains, alongside four vitamins and minerals, to support digestive and immune health. Vegan, dairy-free and gluten-free, they
also contain 45% less sugar than similar bars, are made with 100% natural ingredients and contain nothing artificial.
As the UK’s number one plant-based gut health brand, Biomel’s bars offer a delicious, simple and convenient way for shoppers to increase their fibre intake and support gut health, without relying on supplements or complicated routines.
The proposition is already resonating with shoppers. According to Biomel consumer research, 96% say they would repurchase the Prebiotic Gut Health Bars, while 86% report that they felt a difference after eating one pack.
The findings support Biomel’s strategy of using great-tasting, accessible food and drink formats to bring more consumers into the gut-health category, helping them meet their daily fibre goals in a way that fits naturally into their routines. The bars offer a convenient and enjoyable entry point for shoppers looking to support their gut-health without compromising on taste.
Steven Hegarty, co-founder of Biomel, said: “We know that people understand the importance of looking after their gut health and getting enough fibre, but knowing what to do and actually doing it every day are two different things. That’s why we’ve always focused on making it easier and more appealing for people to support their gut health as part of everyday life.
“The response to our bars has been a strong validation of that approach. People want products that deliver a genuine nutritional benefit, but also taste great and fit naturally into the moments when they already eat. With Peanut Butter and Apple & Cinnamon, we’re giving consumers even more choice when it comes to getting more fibre into their diet and making gut health part of their everyday routine.”
Biomel is currently trusted by more than 320,000 customers and its wider portfolio spans Gut Health Shots & Drinks, Complete Gut advanced nutritional powder, Prebiotic Gut Health Bars and Gut Green Gummies.
To explore the full range of products, visit https://www.biomel.life/collections/our-products

items.body:
Award-winning pet retailer Jollyes Pets is due to open the doors to its latest store in Mansfield, Nottinghamshire, at Oak Tree Centre, Jubilee Way South, NG18 3RT.
Proud to be the UK’s only pet specialist discounter, Jollyes Pets is bringing its commitment to affordable pet care to Mansfield, helping local owners keep the cost of caring for their pets down while household budgets remain under pressure.
To celebrate the opening, customers can get their ‘paws’ on 100 limited-edition goody bags and spin Jollyes’ iconic ‘Wheel of Fur-tune’ for a chance to win prizes, while Jollyes’ mascot, Jolly, will also be on hand to meet and greet visitors. The celebrations will continue on Saturday, with an entertainer in store to add to the family fun.
Marking the official opening, Deputy Mayor of Mansfield, Craig Whitby, will cut the red ribbon alongside some very special canine guests, Hazy, Juke, Ozzy, Jimmy and Buddy. The dogs will attend on behalf of the NFRSA*, Jollyes Pets’ nationwide charity partner. Hazy previously served as a Forensic Evidence Detection Dog with Derbyshire Constabulary, while Juke and Ozzy both served with HMP Nottingham before retiring. Joining them will be active prison detection dogs Jimmy, an English Springer Spaniel, and Buddy, a fox red Labrador.
The brand new store has created 7 jobs for the local community and will be led by store manager Sam Newbold. Sam is looking forward to welcoming Mansfield’s pet owners to the new store and meeting their four-legged friends. A keen animal lover, they have two dogs, Bruce and Toby, and two rabbits, Flin and Albert.
Customers will be able to browse much-loved household names including Pedigree, Whiskas, Harringtons and Felix, alongside specialist pet brands such as Royal Canin and Hill’s, giving pet parents even more choice when it comes to finding the right products for their furry family members.
The store will also stock Jollyes Pets’ own-label ranges, including Lifestage for dogs and cats and Optimum Pet Health, offering big-brand quality at own-label prices and backed by a 100% money-back guarantee.
Pet parents can also expect an extensive selection of raw food, natural treats, alongside toys, treats and accessories – all under one roof.
Sam Newbold, store manager at Jollyes Pets Mansfield, said: “It’s brilliant to be bringing Jollyes Pets to Mansfield and giving local pet owners a new place to discover great value products for their four-legged, feathered and furry friends. Having spent 12 years managing stores, I’m excited to get to know our new team and customers. As a pet lover myself, with two dogs, Bruce and Toby, and two rabbits, Flin and Albert, I know how important our pets are to the family!
“We’re kicking things off with a fun-filled opening weekend, and we can’t wait to welcome the local community into the store, introduce everyone to our mascot Jolly and give visitors the chance to enjoy some freebies and prizes. We’re looking forward to becoming a familiar face in the local pet community!”
The opening will take Jollyes Pets to 129 stores across the UK, with 12 new locations opening since January and a further store set to open in Dunfermline on 5 November, before the end of the year. Over the past three years Jollyes has almost doubled the number of stores across the UK, becoming a clear challenger brand in the UK pet retail market.
