items.body:
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards AI Technology (UK) finalists include John Lewis, FoundIt!, Iceland and Snag
We’re pleased to announce the shortlist for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards AI Technology (UK) category. We received a record number of entries this year and many fantastic examples of technology excellence driving transformative change across the global retail sector.
Check out a rundown of our 2026 shortlists and finalists here.
Congratulations to all those who made it through the initial submission process! It’s now over to our star studded judging panel who will decide the winners to be announced at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London.
The event will be held on Wednesday, 4th November and consist of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.
Click here to book your place at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony on Wednesday, 4th November.
Our 2026 AI Technology (UK) finalists as follows:
Bodycare and PMC
Bodycare was bought out of administration in 2025 and established an ambitious, innovation driven store opening programme to bring its affordable health and beauty offering back to the high street, with AI central to its comeback.
Its ambition is to become an AI first retailer, running store operations through its own proprietary, custom built AI platform, with AI decisioning powering colleague actions and data captured in-store continuously feeding back to sharpen the platform and performance.
Furniture Connect
Furniture Connect is using AI to make more of a furniture retailer’s existing range commercially viable online. The innovation is not simply generating better product images. The real opportunity is using AI to produce the volume and quality of content retailers need, quickly and consistently, across different ecommerce channels.
Goddiva
Goddiva AI is a proprietary AI powered fashion commerce ecosystem developed to transform how customers discover, select and purchase occasionwear online.
Built using OpenAI GPT, LangChain, Pinecone Vector Database, Python, Django, MySQL and Shopify integration, it combines conversational commerce, semantic product discovery, intelligent personalisation, AI Size Finder, Virtual Try-On and automated customer support within one connected platform.
Beyond the customer journey, Goddiva AI powers bestseller analysis, trend forecasting and product performance prediction. The technology has moved beyond experimentation to deliver measurable commercial impact, generating approximately £2.5 million in AI assisted revenue, increasing conversion from 1.4% to 2.5% and reducing returns by 10%.
Iceland and SAI
Iceland partnered with SAI to harness AI to make its stores smarter, safer and easier to run, tackling shrink while improving colleague productivity and operational performance.
SAI’s AI powered platform transforms existing store data into actionable intelligence, enabling Iceland to identify and respond to loss more effectively while giving colleagues the insight they need to take practical action on the shopfloor.
Rather than remaining a proof of concept, the technology is now playing a significant role in Iceland’s highest shrink stores, helping the retailer target the locations responsible for a disproportionate share of total losses and making stores harder environments for theft.
John Lewis and FoundIt!
John Lewis and FoundIt! deployed genuine, scalable AI to transform retail discovery across a complex 170,000-SKU catalogue. The initiative tackled both sides of the journey: helping customers navigate products through intelligent Visual Navigation, while making relevant ranges more discoverable through automated, intent led SEO.
Together, these complementary capabilities created a powerful discovery flywheel, bringing more relevant shoppers to the site, helping them find products more easily and generating an eight-figure commercial benefit.
Levy and Kappture
Levy and Kappture have together, delivered Europe’s largest frictionless store deployment into Manchester United, with seven BRISK bars operating across the historic Old Trafford.
BRISK is Kappture’s proprietary computer vision technology, transforming the traditional bar experience by allowing fans to enter, select and take their products and leave without stopping at a till. AI powered product recognition automatically identifies purchases, while payment and receipts are processed instantly, significantly reducing queues and increasing customer throughput, as well as delivering an excellent fan experience.
The technology is designed from the ground up to operate at the pace and scale required during live sporting events and its performance demonstrates the impact, with one BRISK store reaching a record 21 transactions in a single minute and processing up to 43 products in the same period compared with a maximum of approximately 10 transactions per minute at a traditional bar.
Minimist
Donated second-hand stock is the hardest inventory in retail for AI to handle. Every item is a one-off with no barcode, no SKU and no product data, arriving in unpredictable condition, so none of the catalogue assumptions that make retail AI work apply.
Minimist turns a single photograph of a donated item into a priced, measured, described listing published across eight marketplaces in 30 seconds, against up to 10 minutes by hand. 89% of listings publish with no human edit at all. 73,844 items have been listed this way by 28 charity retailers across the UK, Ireland and Australia, and 31,580 of them have sold.
Snag and Patchworks
Snag, a size inclusive DTC fashion brand shipping to 100+ countries, has taken AI beyond chat and into live retail operations.
Using Claude as the reasoning layer and Patchworks as the execution layer via MCP, Snag's team now runs product and order operations across multiple Shopify storefronts, five warehouse systems, its PLM, Sage 200 and marketplaces through plain language instructions. Patchworks closed the gaps native AI connectors couldn't: it reached systems with no MCP server and unlocked Shopify's Bulk Operations API.
The result: 14,000+ products updated in a single operation, and one of Snag's fastest ever product launches, delivered in around two weeks.

2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Omnichannel Retail Technology Initiative of the Year finalists announced
We’re pleased to announce the shortlist for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Omnichannel Retail Initiative of the Year category. We received a record number of entries this year and many fantastic examples of technology excellence driving transformative change across the global retail sector.
Check out a rundown of our 2026 shortlists and finalists here.
Congratulations to all those who made it through the initial submission process! It’s now over to our star studded judging panel who will decide the winners to be announced at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London.

Our 2026 Omnichannel Retail Initiative of the Year finalists as follows:
Lyzer
Lyzer is a Lisbon-based logistics-as-a-service (LaaS) platform that gives retailers one system for every channel. It brings orders from stores, online shops and marketplaces into one dashboard, assigns picking and delivery work with smart task allocation, and fulfils each order from the nearest store through click-and-collect, home delivery or both.
Guided picking uses optimised store maps, and route optimisation groups deliveries into efficient clusters. Retailers can turn their existing stores into fulfilment hubs: Staples Portugal now offers same-day delivery within four hours. Lyzer has processed over 1.1 million orders worth more than €330 million in GMV.
SaleDock
Celerant ONE is the evolution of Saledock’s all in one retail platform, created to help independent cycling retailers replace disconnected systems with one powerful solution
It unifies PoS, inventory, e-commerce, workshop management, customer data and supplier integrations, simplifying operations across stores and online channels. Developed through direct collaboration with retailers, the platform is intuitive, scalable and tailored to the realities of cycling retail.
Following Saledock’s 2025 acquisition by Celerant Technology, the launch of Celerant ONE combines Saledock’s UK expertise and local team with greater resources and innovation, while preserving the retailer led mission that has guided the business since its founding in 2019.
Sitoo and Paul Smith
Paul Smith has transformed how its stores connect with the wider customer journey through Sitoo Unified Commerce Platform, anchored by PoS.
Rolled out across 30+ stores in eight countries in three months, the solution connects store teams with inventory, customer and cross-channel information in real time. Customers are recognised and rewarded consistently across stores and online, supported by one customer view shared across systems. Associates can move with customers using mobile Point of Service, access inventory beyond the individual store and support ship-from-store. The result is a more connected experience across physical stores and online.
Stellar Global (Marvesting Group) and Samsung
Stellar, part of Marvesting Group, has supported Samsung for over eight years, designing omnichannel strategies that connect in-store experiences with virtual engagement to boost brand loyalty and ROI. Samsung KX isa 20,000 sq ft flagship in London which has been run by Stellar since opening in 2019.
Within this space, Stellar has built end-to-end customer journeys through immersive product experiences, events, workshops, live broadcasts and virtual engagement. For the February 2026 Galaxy S26 Unpacked launch, Samsung KX was transformed into a Korean street watching party, with Stellar delivering a DTC live broadcast, multi-platform review content and 23 hours of TikTok live shopping. Results included a 24% sales uplift, 100% NPS and six million views.
THG Studios
On 26th February, THG Studios delivered the “world’s first AI driven, immersive, shoppable catwalk”, an officially certified world record achievement.
This project deployed a complete, end-to-end AI ecosystem, moving beyond single point solutions. From AI driven creative concepting and a hybrid human-AI model runway, to the ‘Front Row AI’ app that made the event instantly shoppable, THG Studios closed the gap between inspiration and transaction in seconds. It created a new, commercially proven strategy for brand experience, transforming a live marketing event into a measurable, data rich growth engine and setting a new global standard.
VS Labs
VS Labs is the product and innovation arm of Visualsoft, building Shopify apps and in-store tech that connect e-commerce and physical retail into one unified customer experience.
Launched last year, VS Labs develops solutions around the practical challenges retailers face when connecting customer journeys, data and experiences across channels.

Our 2026 Customer Experience Excellence finalists as follows:
Dark’s Bar, Lord’s Cricket Ground
Dark's Bar at Lord’s has transformed hospitality at one of the world’s most iconic sporting venues, combining innovative retail technology with a design sympathetic to Marylebone Cricket Club’s unique heritage.
The solution removes friction from the customer journey while the technology sits quietly in the background, making the experience feel effortless rather than technology led. Faster service and a seamless purchasing journey have contributed to a 35% uplift in units sold. Crucially, innovation has not come at the expense of character: Dark Bar complements the architecture and traditions of Lord’s while meeting modern customer expectations for speed, simplicity and convenience.
Goddiva
Post-Covid, customer expectations have moved beyond simply being able to shop online. Customers increasingly expect digital retail to provide the personalisation, reassurance and individual attention traditionally associated with an in-store experience. Goddiva responded by reimagining occasionwear ecommerce around the individual customer.
AI curated collections adapt around her preferences; intelligent memory recognises her size and past favourites; AI Size Finder helps establish fit; Virtual Try-On lets her see dresses on herself; and personalised alteration recommendations help perfect the final choice. Together, these technologies turn a conventional e-commerce catalogue into an intelligent, evolving digital fitting-room experience designed around each customer.
Hockerty
A Hockerty customer can design a navy suit, a light blue shirt and a camel coat, then see all three on a photo of themselves before a single piece is cut.
That is virtual try-on. Generative AI renders every item in the basket together, from its actual configuration: fabric, cut, colour, lapel, pockets. The same look can be moved to a meeting room, a wedding or a street. It takes 20 to 30 seconds, runs in the browser, and covers the whole range from suits to sneakers, in five languages.
Lloyds Banking Group
Lloyds Rewards is transforming how customers engage with their bank by creating one of the UK's most innovative and rewarding digital experiences.
Available to over ten million eligible customers through Lloyds' digital channels, Rewards combines cashback, challenges, prize draws, retailer discounts and strategic partnerships to help customers save money, discover new brands and be rewarded for everyday activity.
Over the past year, Lloyds has evolved Rewards beyond a traditional cashback proposition into a broader customer engagement platform that delivers meaningful value, greater choice and more personalised experiences. The result is a customer centric innovation that rewards everyday banking in new and engaging ways.
Yours Clothing and Poq
Yours Clothing has worked with poq for seven years, since launching its first native mobile app in 2019.
Rather than treating that success as a one off, Yours Clothing used it as the model for a repeatable, multi-brand mobile commerce strategy: M&Co (2023), Evans (2024), Bad Rhino (2024), Long Tall Sally (2025), Pixie Girl (2025), Yours Clothing Germany (2025), and now the Yours Clothing app (2026) have launched globally on the same proven foundation.
The result is a genuinely scalable approach to omnichannel customer experience - one that delivers a consistently excellent app experience across a diverse portfolio of brands, rather than customer experience excellence being limited to a single flagship.

Ann Summers partnered with PMC to modernise its core IT infrastructure after years of legacy development had left its tech stack complicated, expensive to maintain and difficult to manage, slowing innovation and creating operational friction.
Dunelm and VoCoVo
Dunelm is transforming its in-store communications infrastructure by upgrading from legacy Series 3 to VoCoVo Series 5 Pro Headsets across its stores. The new devices are elevating customer experience, day-to-day reliability and enabling improved comfort, while creating a platform for AI powered features that change the way colleagues operate and respond to customer queries.
At the same time, VoCoVo has integrated real-time operational alerts with Dunelm’s self-checkouts, sending sub-second alerts to colleagues’ headsets when assistance is needed to reduce void transactions and abandoned purchases.
East of England Co-op and Transaction Network Services (TNS)
East of England Co-op operated more than 200 sites on a fragmented, multi-vendor network with failover times of up to 90 seconds. Working with Transaction Network Services (TNS), the retailer deployed TNS Secure SD-WAN to consolidate its connectivity into a single, resilient platform with built-in redundancy.
Failover is now instantaneous, and the retailer has eliminated visible downtime during network incidents. Centralised dashboards have strengthened compliance and security oversight, while a single managed service has reduced operational complexity and delivered estimated savings of 10-15% through vendor consolidation.
Fortnum & Mason and Proximity
For more than 300 years Fortnum & Mason has been known for exceptional personal service. Earlier this year, Proximity and Fortnum & Mason launched 'Fortnum’s Connect' to bring that service to customers wherever they are.
The platform gives store teams a clear view of each customer’s purchases, preferences and conversations, helping them make relevant recommendations, stay in touch beyond the store and serve customers around the world through remote payments and global delivery. Since launching the platform, Fortnum & Mason has built a client book of more than 1,200 high value customers, whose average transaction value is 630% above the company average.
Intersport Elverys and Rezolve Ai
Intersport Elverys, Ireland’s oldest sports retailer, has transformed its online merchandising in partnership with Rezolve Ai; replacing manual, rules-based work with automated product placement across the site and its search results.
MKM Building Supplies and Commerce
MKM has transformed its digital proposition to make purchasing and account management simpler for trade customers, while strengthening the connection between digital and its nationwide branch network.
Working with Commerce, MKM has built a modern, composable commerce platform designed around complex B2B requirements, including personalised pricing, account terms, credit, quotes, invoices and fulfilment. More than 60,000 SKUs are now available online, while the platform is delivering a 4.1% conversion rate and £125 average order value. By modernising its technology while retaining its service led model, MKM has created a more flexible and connected experience for trade customers.
Paul Smith and Sitoo
Paul Smith transformed its international store technology with Sitoo’s cloud native Unified Commerce Platform, anchored by PoS. Rolled out across 30+ stores in eight countries in three months, the project replaced legacy store technology with a connected platform supporting fixed and mobile selling, real-time inventory visibility, customer recognition and cross-channel operations.
The transformation has changed both the customer experience and everyday store operations: associates can spend more time with customers, transactions are faster, store processes have been simplified and manual administration reduced. The result is a modern store platform designed around how Paul Smith wants its teams to serve customers.
The Body Shop and GoPlaces
The Body Shop had deep high street and direct-to-consumer roots but no operating model for social commerce. So GoPlaces built one. It deployed its technology, OnePlace, for the data foundation, created an affiliate creator network at scale, and ran professional live retail from its studios.
GMV grew 15x from launch to peak month, with 177% month-on-month growth through peak gifting season and more than 27 million affiliate video views across 20,400-plus creator videos. A heritage retailer now trades a channel it had no way of measuring before. For The Body Shop this isn’t just marketing campaigns; it’s a new operating model.
THG Ingenuity
In October 2025, THG Ingenuity and Google Cloud announced a strategic partnership. This focused on combining Google Cloud’s generative AI and data analytics products with THG Ingenuity’s end-to-end commerce and fulfilment capabilities with a goal of accelerating product innovation, delivering step change outcomes for customers, and opening new go to market opportunities.
As part of this, THG Ingenuity committed to move its e-commerce and fulfilment platform from four on-premise datacentres to Google Cloud, combining platform modernisation, governance, and future product growth into one operating model.
WHSmith and SOLUM
WHSmith and SOLUM are supporting a new benchmark for travel essentials retail through Newton Pro electronic shelf labels at WHSmith’s flagship stores across Heathrow Terminals 3, 4 and 5.
The stores bring food, health and beauty, technology, pharmacy services and other essentials together in a one stop shop travel destination. Digital shelf-edge communication enables faster, more consistent pricing and promotional updates, helping travellers navigate with confidence while supporting WHSmith’s ambition to make every journey better.

items.body:
FT Live 2026: Future of Retail review: chasing operational improvements and better margins with AI
“The economics of content generation have come down by 20-40% due to AI,” said Gemma Carver, Head of Consumer Industries EMEA, Digital Strategy Group at Adobe, during an FT Live 2026 Future of Retail discussion panel focused on operational efficiencies, which also featured Kingfisher and Lululemon’s ex-CIO, Julie Averill.
“We’ve got retail clients that have put together briefs in three days, compared to the 38 days that it previously took, thanks to AI tools,” said Carver in London on 6th October at the FT Live event.
If you’re putting together a seasonal fashion line, AI can help you with the ordering, shipping and promotion of it in terms of delivering operational and cost saving efficiencies. This can positively impact retailers’ bottom lines if the technology is deployed well. “We’re currently working with a huge well known beverage company that have cut a procedure from six weeks down to eight days, thanks to AI,” added Carver.
She was joined on the discussion panel by Romain Roulleau, Group Digital and E-Commerce Director at Kingfisher, which owns DIY brands, such as B&Q and Screwfix in the UK, and Castorama in France. Its AI tools have previously been covered by RTIH, including a B&Q recommendation engine that is already delivering better conversion rates and £100 million in extra revenue.
“The Spirit personalisation engine was an early win for us,” said Roulleau, who explained that Kingfisher has been tapping AI for the past three to four years. “I’ve been in retail for 25 years and more, including when online and mobile-based commerce first arose,” he added. “I’ve never seen a new technology and channel rise more significantly and faster than AI commerce, which is the new frontier.”
That is interesting but AI in its agentic form is still in its early days, as the panel in London that included Meagan Sobol, Chief Product Officer at Zipline, admitted.
AI is already deployed at numerous retailers in its generative AI, machine learning and various other guises, finding efficiencies and revenue streams via better customer targeting. Roulleau listed how Kingfisher uses it: Personalisation: via its aforementioned Spirit recommendation engine that has driven a £100 million revenue uplift; Pricing and markdown promotions: “We’ve seen a 15% margin improvement due to better markdown promotions,” he said; Digital marketplaces: Kingfisher is aiming for 30% of its business in this segment in future and is already building its ecosystem linkages, explained Roulleau, while stressing getting your product descriptions right to aid discoverability is vital.
Peopleand data need to align to get good AI roll-outs
Julie Averill, former CIO at lululemon where she helped it grow to become a $10 billion business, and now a boardroom advisor that uses the additional knowledge she has from leading Nordstrom’s omnichannel and digital transformation, joined the panel via live video link. “You’ve got to get the data right to get good AI deployments,” she agreed, while adding that people are vital too.
“So many people are afraid of AI. But if your employees aren’t onboard then any roll-out will not work,” said Averill, addressing the elephant in the room that staff fear for their jobs. “You need to get them onboard and explain that it’ll free them up to do other things. Otherwise, they might sabotage a roll-out.”
According to Adobe’s Carver, the importance of brand strength shouldn’t be forgotten either in the coming AI driven commercial revolution where agents may negotiate prices for collectivised consumers and automated machine-to-machine (M2M) payments could offer enhanced convenience, if a trusted and secure environment can be carved out.
Trust and brand strength are crucial
“All of this will be table stakes eventually once everyone has got AI (including on operational end uses),” said Carver. “In that world it is your brand that is the unique selling point.”
Fellow panellist, Meagan Sobol, Chief Product Officer at Zipline, stressed that trust was also vital in the AI era, both in recommendation engines and in transactions. “We have 70+ clients that have already rolled out AI assistants and other tools. But they only work if you’ve got trust,” she said. This applies to consumers and internal staff adoption equally.
“With trust, then AI adoption can follow,” concluded Sobol. “Without that, then it is just another solution.” In other words, the full benefits won’t flow unless you full buy-in and security, governance, data control and mastery, whatever the envisaged end use of the technology.

items.title: These are the two things holding back housebuilding
items.summary: Falling consumer confidence and severe development unviability are hindering housebuilding. We need a comprehensive strategy including regulatory freezes, a shared equity scheme, and planning reforms to tackle the housing crisis, says Gavin Barwell Everybody knows there is a housing crisis – it has been building for the last 50 years. The victims are all around [...]
items.body:
These are the two things holding back housebuilding
Falling consumer confidence and severe development unviability are hindering housebuilding. We need a comprehensive strategy including regulatory freezes, a shared equity scheme, and planning reforms to tackle the housing crisis, says Gavin Barwell
Everybody knows there is a housing crisis – it has been building for the last 50 years. The victims are all around us. A few – fellow citizens reduced to sleeping rough on the streets – are visible, but most are hidden: families stuck in temporary accommodation, millions of young people denied the opportunity to follow in their parents’ footsteps in owning their own home.
That is why, soon after launching in January, Prosper UK set up an expert-led Housing Commission. The new political movement exists to develop ideas for economic growth, of which housebuilding is an important driver, and to occupy a centre ground left vacant for too long. Both mean tackling the housing crisis head on.
My interest in housing goes back to my first job at the Conservative Research Department, and as housing minister in Theresa May’s first government I worked with Sajid Javid on the white paper Fixing Our Broken Housing Market, whose reforms got us close to the holy grail of 300,000 homes a year.
After a couple of years in which Nimby backbenchers held too much sway, we now have a government that wants to build more homes again. It has made some welcome changes to the planning system and increased funding for affordable housing. Yet it is falling far short of its ambition to build 1.5m homes in five years.
What is going wrong? The Commission’s diverse group of industry experts – planners, housebuilders, investors, housing association executives, land agents and economists – identified two things.
First, a lack of consumer confidence is holding back demand. If housebuilders can’t sell or rent out the meagre number of homes they are building, we should hardly be surprised if they don’t build more.
Second, many schemes with planning permission are unviable. It is much more expensive to build an average new home than it was five years ago – £76,000 more since 2020, about half of it cost inflation but half of it regulation, policy and tax such as the Future Homes Standard and nutrient neutrality – but house prices have barely increased, wiping out developers’ margins. A 300-home Build to Rent scheme that would have made an £8m profit in 2020 would now make a £6m loss.
A 300-home Build to Rent scheme that would have made an £8m profit in 2020 would now make a £6m loss
On viability, we recommend a freeze on new regulatory burdens for at least three years, and two tests for every obligation on new housing – whether the cost belongs on new homes, and whether it is proportionate. Section 106 should pay only for what a development needs, not act as a general tax on new homes.
On demand, we propose a strictly targeted, time-limited shared equity scheme, capped at around a fifth of sales per site and funded by an industry access fee. This was the recommendation we agonised over most, but planning changes since the election mean supply can respond, limiting the risk of higher prices. Once these two problems are cracked, the report sets out other recommendations to increase supply, including a National Planning Service for large schemes and councils that are deliberately under-resourcing their planning service or rejecting applications that are compliant with policy. It also proposes a national review of the Green Belt, keeping land that stops towns and cities sprawling and merging and releasing the rest.
Some of this won’t be popular, and anyone looking for simple or quick answers will be disappointed. But that is no excuse for inaction.
I was pleased to see Labour and the Conservatives use their conferences to announce policies the Commission supports – a shared equity scheme for first-time buyers of new homes from Labour and reform of Section 106 from the Conservatives. But our recommendations are not ‘pick n mix’ – boosting demand without increasing supply will help a few people at the expense of everyone else; tackling the viability problem without tackling the demand problem will make little difference. The solution requires attacking the problem from every angle, and the industry experts who wrote the report have shown how.
Gavin Barwell is a former housing minister and Downing Street Chief of Staff, and chaired the Prosper UK Housing Commission.

Grocery technology firm Instacart raids Uber to bring in Emily Dindoffer as Chief of Staff, Advertising
Emily Dindoffer has landed at Instacart as its new Chief of Staff, Advertising. She joins from Uber where she spent the past five years, serving as Chief of Staff, Uber Advertising. In a LinkedIn post, she said: “After nearly five years at Uber, where I had the opportunity to help build and scale Uber Advertising into a global business, I’m incredibly grateful for the people I’ve learned from and the teams I’ve had the privilege of working alongside.”
She added: “A special thank you to my Uber Ads leaders over the years, and to my colleagues around the globe who made the experience so, so meaningful. I’m thrilled to bring those experiences to Instacart and work with Ali Miller (General Manager, Advertising) and the team on what’s ahead.”
Morrisons
Earlier this year, Morrisons launched Instacart’s Caper Cart smart trolleys at a Preston supermarket, marking North American firm Instacart’s first retail partnership in the UK for its AI powered solution. These automatically recognise items as they are placed in the trolley, including weighing fresh produce on the spot.
Customers can bag items as they shop, saving time throughout the trip and making checkout quicker and easier. The trolley's touchscreen displays a running basket total to help customers stay on budget, makes relevant product recommendations, and enables them to scan their Morrisons More Card to access loyalty savings and promotions throughout their shop. At the end of their trip, they scan the barcode displayed on the trolley's screen at a dedicated Caper checkout lane to complete payment.
"Caper smart trolleys represent a new era for in-store grocery shopping - one where the physical store is as intelligent and personalised as the best online experience," said David McIntosh, Chief Connected Stores Officer at Instacart. “Customers want technology that helps them stay on budget and discover products they love, and Caper smart trolleys deliver both, directly in the aisle. We're proud to bring this to the UK for the first time through our partnership with Morrisons, who share our belief that technology should make the weekly shop not just easier, but genuinely more enjoyable."
"Our customers are at the heart of everything we do, and we're always looking for ways to make their weekly shop easier, more rewarding, and more enjoyable, to give them more reasons to shop at Morrisons," said Gordon Macpherson, Productivity Director at Morrisons. “Caper smart trolleys do exactly that, giving customers real-time visibility of their spending, instant access to their More Card savings, and a more seamless experience in the aisle. We're proud to be the first UK retailer to bring this technology to our customers, and we look forward to seeing how shoppers in Preston and across Lancashire respond to this innovative new trolley in this in-store trial.”

Focus on flexible payment options for e-commerce merchants as Ecommpay adds Klarna to its platform
Payments platform, Ecommpay, has added buy now pay later big hitter, Klarna, to its line up. “Flexible payment options are fundamental to a strong checkout experience for e-commerce merchants and Klarna has been a popular choice for consumers and businesses,” says Roman Tazetdinov, Head of Strategic Partnerships at Ecommpay. “Used by millions of shoppers every month, we are confident adding Klarna to the Ecommpay payment platform will deliver real conversion gains for our merchants.”
"Shoppers today expect to pay their way: no faff, no friction, no nasty surprises," says Klarna Country Manager UK & Ireland Marc O'Fathaigh. "Ecommpay is a natural fit: we both believe good ways to pay should be available to everyone. Through a single integration, this partnership puts Klarna in front of merchants worldwide, expanding our reach and giving millions of shoppers more control over their money."
Covering retail, travel and hospitality, FinTech, mobility, digital goods and insurance, Ecommpay merchants gain access to Klarna’s payment options including Pay in Full, Pay in 3 and Pay in 4 instalments, Pay in 30 days, and longer-term financing, via one integration with no extra technical work or third-party systems needed.
“We know that many shoppers actively look for Klarna at checkout,” adds Tazetdinov. “Adding it to the Ecommpay payment platform gives merchants access to a large and engaged market, reducing hesitation at the point of purchase and giving customers another payment option at checkout. And it can be added to a merchant’s wider payment set-up in a single integration, eliminating unnecessary operational overhead.”

items.body:
Jingle tills! Black Friday through Cyber Monday weekend sales set to surpass $85 billion in USA
US retail sales over the Black Friday through Cyber Monday weekend are expected to top $85 billion, accounting for 8.5% of 2026 holiday sales, according to Bain & Company research. Sales growth during the weekend is set to rise 8.75% year over year, outpacing Bain's total holiday season growth forecast of 4.5%.
Using proprietary credit card data from Pyxis, Bain's consumer intelligence division, its report finds that Black Friday is likely to remain the leading sales day of the holiday season as consumers continue to treat it as the official kick-off. In fact, 64% of consumers surveyed will be out in force on Black Friday, up from 55% in 2025. Cyber Monday has also continued to gain popularity and is expected to crack the top five sales days this year, as more shoppers say they will do their holiday shopping online. 44% of consumers surveyed plan to shop Cyber Monday, compared to 41% last year.
Bains’s survey of US consumers finds that 70% plan to shop Black Friday and/or Cyber Monday, up from 64% last year, and more than 90% are looking to do so on either those days or another major sales event. The final two weekends before Christmas carry just as much weight, however. In 2025, six of the top ten sales days landed in that window. Overall, Bain forecasts US holiday sales will top $1 trillion for the first time, driven by in-store sales and rising e-commerce.
"Black Friday and Cyber Monday are becoming increasingly important battlegrounds for retailers, especially as US consumers prioritise value and deal heavy shopping days," says Aaron Cheris, Global Head of Retail at Bain & Company. "Retailers that capitalise on these crucial sales days with personalised promotions, can’t miss events, and targeted campaigns will set themselves up well for the rest of the holiday shopping season."

items.title: We’ll pull Neet support if Healey hikes taxes, warns boss of B&Q owner Kingfisher
items.summary: The boss of B&Q-owner Kingfisher has warned John Healey that the FTSE 100 firm may have to pull its support for unemployed young people if the Chancellor hikes taxes. Thierry Garnier, the retail group’s chief executive, wrote in City AM that the Chancellor must exempt shops from the highest bracket of business rates at the [...]
items.body:
We’ll pull Neet support if Healey hikes taxes, warns boss of B&Q owner Kingfisher
The boss of B&Q-owner Kingfisher has warned John Healey that the FTSE 100 firm may have to pull its support for unemployed young people if the Chancellor hikes taxes.
Thierry Garnier, the retail group’s chief executive, wrote in City AM that the Chancellor must exempt shops from the highest bracket of business rates at the Budget later this month or risk plunging more young people into unemployment.
Garnier said retailers, who are among the highest employers of young people in the country, want to tackle the Neets crisis but will not be able to if their costs keep rising.
“We share the Government’s concerns about the number of young people not in employment, education or training (NEET), and we have committed to offering work experience placements at B&Q and Screwfix to help tackle this,” he said. “While we want to keep doing this, whether we can depends on what the Chancellor decides in this Budget.”
Garnier’s intervention comes as retail bosses ramp up pressure on Healey to cut taxes on the industry and help them support the government’s pledge to deliver “growth in every postcode”.
The British Retail Consortium, which represents the industry’s top businesses including B&Q, has urged the Chancellor to unwind some of the hikes to employer national insurance contributions (NICs) implemented by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves.
Garnier said tackling business rates is the “single biggest opportunity for the Chancellor to help retailers keep investing” in the UK.
Retailers have long said business rates are an outdated tax which disadvantage high street firms in comparison to online sellers. They have urged the Labour government to stick to its election manifesto pledge to “replace” the tax system.
Healey must ‘level playing field’
The Kingfisher boss said: “If the government is committed to its growth strategy, it must reform this long-outdated business rates system and level the playing field between bricks and mortar shops and online-only operators.
“We understand the Chancellor faces difficult choices, but with a new administration comes new opportunities for change. Our message to deliver growth is therefore simple: take shops out of paying the higher rate.”
On Tuesday, the BRC and top retailers including Sainsbury’s and Tesco met with the Chancellor to set out their demands ahead of the Budget, which included business rates reform and action on Neets.
Kingfisher, which also owns Screwfix, lifted its profit forecast last month after its pivot toward trade customers delivered growing sales.
In May, Garnier announced his intention to depart Kingfisher after being poached by Dutch-Belgian retail giant Ahold Delhaize. On Tuesday, it was announced that he will be succeeded by Sebastian Gundel in February.
The Treasury was contacted for comment.

items.title: Convenience stores reach £10bn National Lottery Good Causes milestone
items.summary: Independent retailers across the UK have raised more than £10bn for Good Causes by selling National Lottery tickets, new data from Allwyn UK, operator of The National Lottery, has revealed. The milestone figure has been raised by corner shops across the UK since The National… This story continues at Convenience stores reach £10bn National Lottery Good Causes milestone Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The milestone figure has been raised by corner shops across the UK since The National Lottery launched in 1994.
On average, 23p of every pound spent on The National Lottery goes to Good Causes, which has supported more than 680,000 projects across arts, community, heritage and sports since its launch in 1994.
Today, over 22,000 independent retailers sell National Lottery tickets and scratchcards, and of those, 1,623 shops have raised more than £500,000, 469 have raised more than £1m, and 28 have broken the £2m mark.
Remarkably, two shops have each raised more than £3m for Good Causes.
Three such retailers, located in Kent, Wales and West Yorkshire, have been recognised as part of Allwyn’s ‘Local Retail Champions’ initiative, each receiving a visit from a famous face that has benefited from National Lottery funding.
A further six stores, located in Bristol, Manchester, Belfast, Glasgow, Ilkeston and Gateshead will feature in a secondary phase of the campaign.
Alastair Ruxton, chief impact officer, Allwyn UK, said: “Most people in the UK live within half a mile of a Lottery funded Good Cause project, in no small part due to the extraordinary efforts of independent retailers who sell National Lottery tickets.
“The remarkable £10 billion local retailers have raised for Good Causes around the country has helped train Olympic and Paralympic athletes, fund award-winning British films and our world-renowned brilliant museums and galleries, as well as supporting thousands of vital community, education and heritage projects.”
Community Champions
Monty Dipoti, owner of Todmorden News in West Yorkshire, has raised more than £2.3m for Good Causes since taking over the shop 16 years ago.
He was visited by Yorkshire local Nicola Adams, the first female boxer to become an Olympic champion after winning gold at London 2012 who was supported throughout her career with National Lottery funding.
Dipoti and Adams visited Northern Powerhouse Boxing Academy, the UK’s first women-led boxing club, which has received £250,000 of Lottery funding between 2018-2025 and helped to restore a flood damaged community building that had stood empty for ten years.
Kuljit Athwal, owner of Premier Grand Avenue Stores in Cardiff, has raised more than £1m for Good Causes during his time running the shop. He was treated to a surprise visit by presenter and actress Joanna Page (top picture).
Together they visited Ministry of Life Education (MOL Education), a National Lottery-funded education and outreach provider based in Cardiff that supports young people who are disengaged from mainstream education and are at risk of not being in employment, education, or training. It has received £568,000 of National Lottery funding to provide personalised learning that helps young people build confidence, develop practical skills and gain accredited qualifications.
Steve Weight has run Borough Green Stores in Kent for 32 years, raising more than £1.4m for Good Causes in that time. He was surprised by local hero Matt Weston, double Olympic gold medal skeleton racer at the 2026 Winter Olympic Games, who grew up just down the road in Sevenoaks and benefited from funding through UK Sport’s Elite Athletes programme.
Weston visited Charlie’s Angels Kitchens, a local not-for-profit organisation focused on tackling both food poverty and food waste, that has received £20k of Lottery funding thanks to retailers like Weight.
Nicola Adams said: “I would not have won Olympic gold were it not for the funding made possible by incredible independent retailers like Monty – they are the heartbeat of their local communities.
“Thanks to their hard work, Good Causes like Northern Powerhouse Boxing Academy get the support they need, guiding the way for the next generation of Olympians.”
Joanna Page said: “The funds raised by corner shops around the country are vital for the UK’s arts and creative industries. I grew up going into shops just like Kuljit’s, they are the backbone of our high streets. Seeing the incredible work done by MOL, funded by the hard work of people like Kuljit, is an inspiration.”
Matt Weston said: “I should really give one of my gold medals to Steve. I cannot overstate the importance of the funding I’ve received from The National Lottery, and shop owners like Steve deserved a huge amount of credit for their role in raising it. He really is a local hero.”
The campaign is supported by Allwyn’s Social Value Fund that the company has committed to invest in social value initiatives.

In September, The Times reported that Treasury officials were modelling higher rates of tax on gaming machines, with a government source describing gambling tax rises as “definitely on the table again”. items.body:
When Chancellor John Healey delivers his first Budget on 28 October, gambling taxes are expected to be on the agenda again. In September, The Times reported that Treasury officials were modelling higher rates of tax on gaming machines, with a government source describing gambling tax rises as “definitely on the table again”. The Treasury’s only public line is that decisions are made at fiscal events.
For retailers, this is not a niche issue. Betting shops, arcades, bingo halls, pubs with fruit machines and the convenience counter selling lottery tickets all sit either in the firing line or next door to it. Here is what has already been decided, what is being discussed, and what to watch for on the day.
What has already been decided
Most of the online side was settled a year ago. The November 2025 Budget, legislated in Finance Act 2026, made these changes:
- Remote Gaming Duty, the tax on online casino profits, rose from 21% to 40% on 1 April 2026.
- Online betting gets a new 25% rate within General Betting Duty from 1 April 2027. Bets on UK horseracing, self-service terminals in shops, spread bets and pool bets are excluded.
- Betting in shops stays at 15%.
- Bingo Duty on land-based bingo was abolished from 1 April 2026.
The government also dropped plans for a single online duty and gave the Gambling Commission an extra £26m over three years to tackle illegal gambling. According to the government’s own figures, the package raises £810m in 2026–27, rising to £1.155bn by 2030–31.
With online casino duty already doubled, attention has moved to the high street.
Machine Games Duty is the decision that matters most
Machine Games Duty is charged on the takings from gaming machines, and its current rates have not changed since 2015:
- 5% on machines costing up to 20p a play with a top prize of £10.
- 20% on most other machines, where a play costs no more than £5.
- 25% where a single play can cost more than £5.
It raised £641m in 2025–26, according to HMRC.
The bands are set by stake and prize, not by machine category. So a betting-shop B2 or B3 machine and a pub’s Category C fruit machine currently both pay the 20% standard rate.
The most detailed proposal on the table comes from the Social Market Foundation. Its June 2026 report calls for a new 40% band for Category B machines only, the type found in betting shops, casinos and adult gaming centres. Category C would stay at 20% and Category D at 5%. The think tank estimates this would raise £275m–£458m a year. Its stated logic is to match the 40% rate already paid on online casino games.
The Times’ sources also pointed to possible carve-outs. One Labour source was quoted as saying the Prime Minister “hates adult gaming centres” but “loves bingo halls and pubs”. A rise aimed at one machine category would need new definitions, so the design of any change may matter as much as the headline rate.
What the industry says it would cost
The trade has moved quickly to put numbers on a rise. All of the figures below are industry estimates, not official forecasts.
- Betting and Gaming Council: modelling it commissioned from EY suggests up to 1,470 betting shop closures, 34 casinos and around 16,000 jobs at risk. It forms the basis of the trade body’s “Back Our Betting Shops” campaign.
- Entain: chief executive Stella David wrote to the Prime Minister in September warning that a 40% standard rate would add around £100m a year to the Ladbrokes and Coral owner’s UK retail costs. The company launched its “What’s at Stake” campaign this month.
- Betfred: founder Fred Done has said 495 of the chain’s shops would close at a 40% rate, and has gone as far as predicting that “by 2030 we will have no betting shops”.
- Regulus Partners: analysis reported by trade press estimates a doubled rate would cost a typical shop around £45,000 a year. It warns of up to 4,000 closures within three years and £92m a year lost to British racing.
Rank has said a third of its venues would be at risk, and the arcade trade body Bacta opposes any rise.
The case on the other side
Not everyone accepts those projections. The Guardian has pointed out that Betfred has warned of around 1,000 closures since 2019, while its estate actually shrank by about 330 over the period. It also notes that arcade takings have kept rising, which suggests customers moving between venue types rather than a sector in freefall. Paddy Power co-founder Stewart Kenny has called the warnings scaremongering.
The industry also argues that higher taxes will push customers towards unlicensed offshore websites. This raises an important distinction between overseas licensing and UK authorisation. Curaçao betting sites operate under a different regulatory framework, but holding a Curaçao licence alone does not authorise a bookmaker to serve customers in Great Britain. The regulator’s evidence on illegal gambling is more cautious. In November 2025, the Gambling Commission concluded its series on illegal online gambling. It published no estimate of the illegal market’s size and found no evidence of sustained growth in people using illegal sites. Higher figures in circulation come from industry and third-party analysts.
Why landlords and neighbouring retailers should care
Great Britain had 5,617 betting shops in March 2026, down 3.6% (208 shops) on the year, according to the Gambling Commission’s latest industry statistics. Closures are already under way before any Budget decision:
- Betfred announced 132 closures on 31 July.
- Evoke, owner of William Hill, has been reported to be closing around 270 shops.
- Flutter is reviewing up to 100 Paddy Power shops.
Policy is pulling in the same direction. Betting shops were excluded from the lower business rates multipliers for retail, hospitality and leisure introduced in April 2026. The government has also said it intends to scrap the Gambling Act’s “aim to permit” principle, which limits councils’ ability to refuse new gambling premises. Adult gaming centres would need planning permission from 2027, subject to consultation, as set out in August.
For landlords on secondary parades, the question is not only whether betting shops close but what replaces them. Entain, for its part, is investing in the shops it has kept.
Pubs, arcades and the convenience counter
Pub fruit machines pay the 20% standard rate, with the duty paid by the tenant. A blanket increase would therefore land on pubs as well as bookmakers. A rise limited to Category B machines would leave them untouched, which would fit with the 20% business rates cut for pubs from 2027/28 announced in July.
Arcades look more exposed. Gambling Commission figures show arcade takings up 10.7% to £800m in the last financial year, and adult gaming centres are the venues most often singled out in reports of the Treasury’s thinking.
For convenience retailers, the lottery appears safe for now. Lottery Duty has stood at 12% since 1994, and no change has been proposed. Allwyn’s £10 scratchcard pilot, which pays retailers 60p a card, continues regardless.
All licensed operators also pay the statutory gambling levy introduced in April 2025, at 0.5% of yield for land-based betting and 0.2% for arcades and bingo.
The player-protection question
Whatever happens to tax, operators’ duties to identify and act on signs of gambling harm stay the same. As more of the transaction in betting shops moves to self-service terminals, more of that work falls to technology as well as the staff behind the counter.
For staff and customers alike, the options are summarised in this guide to responsible gambling. It covers everything from deposit limits and cooling-off periods online to the multi-operator self-exclusion scheme (MOSES) used in betting shops, alongside GamStop for online sites.
What should retailers watch for on 28 October?
- Machine Games Duty: whether it rises at all, and whether any increase is limited to Category B machines.
- Carve-outs: any exemptions for pubs, bingo halls or clubs.
- Online betting: whether the 25% rate due in April 2027 is touched, although no one is currently calling for a delay.
- Business rates: changes to reliefs, including the review of reliefs for businesses the government says do not contribute positively to high streets.
- Councils: the timetable for new local powers over gambling premises.
The decisions themselves may come down to a handful of lines in the Red Book. For the high streets where betting shops, arcades and pubs sit side by side, their effects will be felt for considerably longer.
Gambling products are for adults aged 18 and over. Free, confidential support is available 24 hours a day from the National Gambling Helpline on 0808 8020 133.

The Dunmurry shop opens with a modern look and comfortable seating and will be open daily from 6:30am – 6:30pm.

Brian Donaldson, CEO of The Maxol Group, said: “Greggs is a new and exciting addition to Maxol’s food to go offer. items.title: UK high street bosses urge chancellor to cut cost of employing young people
items.summary: Retailers call on John Healey to reduce national insurance contributions threshold in his first budget Some of the UK’s biggest retailers and hospitality businesses, including Tesco, Costa Coffee and the Co-op, have met John Healey to urge him to cut the cost of employing young people in his first budget. At the No 11 event on Tuesday morning, the chancellor heard from sector leaders – including the boss of Marks & Spencer, Stuart Machin, and Sainsbury’s chief executive, Simon Roberts – about the impact of the rise in employers’ national insurance contributions (Nics). Continue reading...
items.body:
Some of the UK’s biggest retailers and hospitality businesses, including Tesco, Costa Coffee and the Co-op, have met John Healey to urge him to cut the cost of employing young people in his first budget.
At the No 11 event on Tuesday morning, the chancellor heard from sector leaders – including the boss of Marks & Spencer, Stuart Machin, and Sainsbury’s chief executive, Simon Roberts – about the impact of the rise in employers’ national insurance contributions (Nics).
Businesses want a partial reversal of the surprise move by Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, who lowered the earnings threshold at which they start to pay Nics from £9,100 to £5,000 a year. They argue the change contributed to the plunge in the number of high street jobs for young people and part-time workers and a rise in youth unemployment.
They want the Nics threshold raised to £6,000, arguing this would help create jobs and ease inflation pressures on high streets.
Retail and hospitality firms also hope Healey will ease the burden of business rates, and one source close to the meeting said they were optimistic on both fronts. “It felt like they were listening,” the source said.
Healey has vowed to ease the cost of doing business amid mounting pressures on firms from rising energy bills.
Another attender, Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the British Retail Consortium trade body which represents most big retailers, said: “Retail is a major driver of growth, supporting jobs, investment and communities across the country, and providing vital first jobs and career opportunities for young people.
“But after whacking up retailers’ taxes by 20% in two years, including an extra £6.5bn in new employment costs, any new costs will be paid by consumers at the till and make it harder for retailers to create jobs.
“The chancellor recognised these pressures, and we had a positive discussion about our shared ambition for growth and tackling youth unemployment. His first budget is the chance to turn that ambition into action by easing costs, making tax fairer and unlocking investment.”
Meanwhile it was reported that Healey has rejected calls from Labour MPs and thinktanks to use the budget to equalise the rates at which capital gains and income from work are taxed.
He has come under pressure to increase the rates of capital gains tax (CGT), which is levied on the sale of assets – including second homes and shares – at significantly lower rates than wages.
In her first budget in 2024, Reeves increased the rate of CGT from 10% to 18% for basic-rate taxpayers, and from 20% to 24% for higher-rate taxpayers. That compares with a 20% basic rate of income tax, a 40% higher rate and 45% additional rate for top earners.
Economists have suggested an equalisation of the rates could raise £11.3bn a year for the exchequer. However, according to the Financial Times, Healey has dismissed such calls because of fears it could deter inward investment, but may yet opt for a smaller increase in CGT short of equalisation.
It comes after senior Labour figures floated CGT increases among options to repair the government finances while funding priorities ranging from public services, support for households and long-term infrastructure projects.
The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, suggested the idea of equalisation during his ill-fated May pitch to be the party leader as a “wealth tax that works”.
And the first secretary, Louise Haigh, a close ally of Andy Burnham, argued in an article in the journal Renewal in May – while on the backbenches before her return to cabinet – that CGT rates should be “brought closer to income tax rates”.
A Treasury spokesperson said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

items.body:
Loyalty to both retailers and brands is weakest among 45-54-year-olds as just 35% of the age group describe themselves as financially comfortable, according to new research from IGD.
IGD’s shopper research shows financial pressure peaks in mid-life, with housing costs and bills consuming almost half (49%) of monthly spending among 45-54-year-olds. In comparison, 46% of both 18-24 and 25-34-year-olds describe themselves as financially comfortable, with household bills taking up 32% and 34% respectively.
At the same time, loyalty to grocery retailers falls to 55% among 55-64-year-olds, the lowest level of any age group, while loyalty to grocery brands reaches its lowest point among 45-54-year-olds at 51%.
Caroline Young, head of shopper insight at IGD, said: “Many mid-life shoppers are becoming the ‘sandwich generation’, balancing mortgages, rising household bills, children and ageing parents.
“What this means for retailers and brands is mid-life shoppers need the strongest reassurance that they’re spending their money well. That’s balancing price with quality, freshness, availability and reliability, rather than competing on price alone.”
Pressure and loyalty collide in mid-life
IGD’s research shows pressure intensifies through mid-life as shoppers juggle multiple financial and caring responsibilities.
Among 45-54-year-olds, 23% are caring for children under 18, while 18% are also caring for parents or parents-in-law. The combination of housing costs, family responsibilities and wider financial pressures leaves many consumers balancing competing demands on their time and budgets.
Financial confidence follows a similar pattern. Shopper confidence remains positive among younger adults before turning negative after age 45, highlighting a clear divide in financial outlook across age groups.
The loyalty challenge for retailers and brands
IGD’s findings suggest value is increasingly becoming a retention strategy rather than an acquisition strategy. Shoppers aged 45-64 are among the most focused on keeping costs down, but they are also more likely than average to try to balance cost with quality rather than simply buy the cheapest products available.
The research indicates that value is increasingly linked to trust, reliability and helping households make stretched budgets go further.
For financially pressured shoppers, value extends beyond price. Products that last longer, reduce waste and are reliably available are becoming increasingly important measures of whether a purchase represents good value.
The research also finds that shoppers with caring responsibilities are significantly more likely than non-carers to be dissatisfied with product availability, highlighting the growing importance of reliability alongside price.
An early signal of future shopper needs
While these pressures are visible among mid-life shoppers today, IGD believes they may provide an early indication of how value expectations are likely to evolve across the wider grocery market.
With the UK’s 65+ population forecast to grow from 13.8 million to 16.2 million by 2035, needs such as value, quality, freshness and availability are likely to become increasingly influential across the wider grocery market.
A free sample of IGD’s report, ‘What will matter to shoppers in 2035’, is available on the IGD website.

The retailer has continued its momentum […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Following today’s release of Victorian Plumbing’s figures for the 12 months ending 30 September 2026; Matt Walton, senior retail analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers his view: “Victorian Plumbing continues to outperform the bathroom furniture market through prudent investment and a focus on price competitiveness. The retailer has continued its momentum from its first half, when sales grew 10.5%, with full-year revenue up by around 11% to £344m. These results include strong growth from tiles and flooring, which increased by circa 76% as consumer awareness improved, as well as £7m from Sovereign Transport Services, which Victorian Plumbing acquired in January 2026. Once the above revenue streams as well as growth in trade are stripped out, revenue grew by c.5.0% for the year meaning that Victorian Plumbing has comfortably extended its lead atop the bathroom furniture market, which grew by 0.8% over its financial year. This performance is more impressive considering the difficulties that B&Q has experienced within bathroom, and Topps Tiles described the tiling market as “challenging” in its recent full-year results.
“Although trade sales increased 6% for the overall year, this division’s proportion of sales remains similar to FY2023/24 at around 23%, indicating that there is still significant opportunity for Victorian Plumbing within this market. The retailer remains well placed to make these gains as it continues to develop its trade offer as third-party financing and a later next-day delivery cut off were introduced at the end of its first half. The use of targeted radio campaigns and sporting event sponsorship will maintain awareness among these customers which will offer the retailer a more consistent revenue stream.
“Victorian Plumbing’s adjusted profit before tax has finished ahead of market expectations, though has remained largely static, rising by just 0.9% to around £22m mainly due to a £4m loss from MFI. This offset a £2.2m improvement at the Victorian Plumbing fascia, which delivered c.£26m adjusted profit before tax. While MFI’s loss is to be expected early in its journey (and MFI recorded £3m in revenue for FY2025/26), one of the first challenges for new CEO Stephnie Judge will be how to build a strong identity among shoppers, with MFI having little traction among younger shoppers and potentially negative perceptions among older shoppers.
“Shoppers continue to be cautious about making bigger-ticket purchases, which is also stifling performance for Victorian Plumbing. Overall order numbers grew by 13% for the period but this was counterbalanced by the average order value declining by 5%. A factor behind the order value decline is the exceptional uplift from lower-priced tiles and flooring in FY25/26, but growth for tiles and flooring slightly cooled in the second half, while the decline in overall average order value accelerated from the -3% it recorded during its first half. The higher cost of living for food, fuel and utility costs following the invasion of Iran has undoubtedly contributed to order values being lower as shoppers make smaller refreshes and replacement purchases. As such, developing its trade offer further is essential for Victorian Plumbing to maintain its current trajectory.”

items.title: Morrisons sales rise faster than those at would-be bidder Sainsbury's for first time in five years amid signs of recovery
items.summary: The last time Morrisons did better than Sainsbury's on quarterly sales growth was months before its £7billion takeover by a private equity firm in October 2021.
items.body:
Morrisons sales rise faster than those at would-be bidder Sainsbury's for first time in five years amid signs of recovery
Sales growth at Morrisons has exceeded would-be-bidder Sainsbury's for the first time in five years as the struggling supermarket sees signs its turnaround is starting to pay off.
The last time Morrisons did better than Sainsbury's on quarterly sales growth was months before its £7billion takeover by a private equity firm in October 2021.
Britain’s second largest grocer Sainsbury’s called off merger talks with its smaller rival Morrisons earlier this year, it was revealed this month.
Sales at Morrisons increased 1.1 per cent in the three months to October 3, surpassing the 0.7 per cent jump at Sainsbury’s, according to closely watched figures from market researchers NielsenIQ.
But it now holds 8.3 per cent of the market, down slightly from the 8.4 per cent the same time last year.
Chief executive Rami Baitiéh, who took over as chief executive in November 2023, said last month that there was 'clear evidence that our strategy is delivering and that we remain on track'.
Britain’s second largest grocer Sainsbury’s called off merger talks with its smaller rival Morrisons earlier this year.
Baitiéh has overseen price cuts to reverse Morrisons' fortunes after losing market share to German discounters Aldi and Lidl.
But he admitted that trading conditions ‘remained highly competitive’ amid a price war between major supermarkets that has seen similar price cutting schemes.
The business has been struggling since it was taken over by private equity firm Clayton Dubilier & Rice (CD&R) in 2021 and last year its debt pile hit £7.5billion.
Morrisons had hailed its strongest sales growth for a year as the World Cup helped to bring shoppers through its doors. It said that hot weather and the football tournament lifted group like-for-like sales by 3.2 per cent over the 13 weeks to July 26.
In August, Morrisons launched a new ‘unbeatable prices’ pledge across more than 500 everyday products. It promises that the products covered will cost the same or less than at Aldi, Asda, Lidl, Sainsbury’s and Tesco, which ‘has already had a positive impact.’
Earlier this month, it was reported that Sainsbury’s held talks with Morrisons about a potential merger between November 2025 and February this year, according to the Financial Times.
But Sainsbury’s ended the talks and there are no active discussions, the report said.
A merger would be one of the biggest supermarket deals in over five years, creating a grocery giant with just over 22 per cent of market share.
Leader Tesco has a 26.3 per cent share, according to the same research.
Any takeover of Morrisons would be looked at by the competition watchdog and probably involve Sainsbury’s having to sell some shops.

items.body:
Danish confectionery brand LAKRIDS BY BÜLOW is proud to announce the opening of its 50th store worldwide, at the iconic Battersea Power Station in London. The milestone marks a significant moment in the brand’s continued international growth and further strengthens its presence in the UK, one of its fastest-growing markets.
The new store will bring LAKRIDS BY BÜLOW’s distinctive range of gourmet chocolate-coated liquorice to one of London’s most prominent retail, leisure and cultural destinations. Visitors at Battersea Power Station will be able to explore the full product range, including limited edition flavours, alongside in-store tastings designed to introduce both existing customers and those new to liquorice to the brand’s unique flavour combinations and approach to the category.
Since launching in the UK in 2021, LAKRIDS BY BÜLOW has steadily expanded its retail footprint, with London playing a key role in its growth. The brand has established a presence through store openings on Monmouth Street, Westfield London and Selfridges, alongside retail listings with John Lewis and Liberty London. The opening inside the Grade II* listed Power Station marks the latest chapter in LAKRIDS BY BÜLOW’s ambition to make the world love liquorice.
CEO at LAKRIDS BY BÜLOW, Fredrik Nilsson, states: “Fifty stores is a milestone we’re incredibly proud of, and it feels particularly fitting to celebrate it in London. Since landing on UK shores we’ve seen great interest in our approach to liquorice, crafted just outside Copenhagen, and have continued to build our presence across the city. Battersea Power Station has become a popular destination for shopping, dining and leisure in London, and its iconic character makes it a natural home for LAKRIDS BY BÜLOW. We’re delighted to be opening our doors here, introducing our brand to even more Londoners. LAKRIDS BY BÜLOW was founded with a simple ambition: to make the world love liquorice, and this new store gives us another opportunity to bring that ambition to life.”
Renee Moran, head of asset management at Battersea Power Station, said: “We’re delighted to welcome LAKRIDS BY BÜLOW to Battersea Power Station as the brand celebrates the opening of its 50th store at our riverside neighbourhood. Renowned for their distinctive gourmet liquorice and chocolate, LAKRIDS BY BÜLOW is a perfect addition to our growing retail lineup, and the new store will provide visitors with another exciting offering to discover when shopping inside the Power Station.”
The new LAKRIDS BY BÜLOW store will open its doors on Thursday 15th October on the Ground floor of Turbine Hall A in Battersea Power Station, London, SW11 8AH.

items.title: Employees all over the world find themselves monitored by AI at work
items.summary: The latest example of workers under surveillance comes from Co-op, a British consumer co-operative that runs thousands of businesses This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here . Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you while moving laundry from the washer to the dryer, wishing a robot could do the task for me. Today in tech, we’re talking about workers and AI. Continue reading...
items.body:
Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you while moving laundry from the washer to the dryer, wishing a robot could do the task for me. Today in tech, we’re talking about workers and AI.
Workers under surveillance
Employees across the globe are increasingly finding themselves minutely monitored in their workplaces, with tiny changes in their behaviors resulting in negative performance evaluations.
The latest example of workers under surveillance and bristling at it comes from Co-op, which operates supermarkets, undertakers, insurance and legal services companies in the UK. The company implemented an automated listening technology that rates every phone call some of them make to customers.
In a system described as “oppressive and dystopian” by a whistleblower, Co-op Legal Services is using AI models to record, analyze and award a percentage score for interactions between agents and customers seeking advice about probate, wills and estates.
“You are being watched,” said a Co-op worker who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity.
Read more: ‘Dystopian’: Co-op becomes latest firm to put staff under AI surveillance
The Co-op said it did not recognize the criticism and said its probate advisers were highly engaged.
Resentment of workers’ treatment is already translating into policy, a break from the sluggishness of most technology regulations. Across the Atlantic and the continental United States, California governor Gavin Newsom signed laws into effect last week that prohibit certain types of workplace surveillance.
California’s laws aim to target workplace surveillance measures like heat maps that track employees’ movements, including how long they spend in the bathroom, or having their emotional states monitored. Amazon warehouse workers have previously complained about being timed on their bathroom breaks, for example. And at Kaiser Permanente, a California hospital chain, nurses have said automated systems rated their tone of voice in patient interactions.
Read more: California’s new laws target workers’ biggest fear of AI taking their jobs
***
Tell us: Are you being watched at work?
Tell us: have you been monitored or assessed by AI at work?
Silicon Valley on screen
Artificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satire
The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg
Whom does AI benefit?
Two stories recently published in the Guardian’s Reworked series pose the question: who is AI enriching?
The first story details how the AI boom is leaving women out of the single largest engine of growth in the US economy. One visible example: Donald Trump’s all-male summit of AI leaders last week: not a single woman in sight as the president preached the power of “superintelligence”.
“We’re talking about who captures a major new source of economic mobility,” said Felicia Newhouse, founder of AI Powered Women, an organization that promotes women’s participation and leadership in AI. “The deepest risk is that a participation gap becomes a power gap.”
Read more: The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behind
Across AI-related occupations, the median pay of men is $45,000 higher than that of women, partly due to the types of jobs men and women are more likely to have, according to research by LinkedIn: men are still typically hired for higher-paying roles in the AI industry.
When pitching investors, one female co-founder of an AI startup said she has found through trial and error that she and her male co-founder are more likely to get an investment if he does the pitching.
Another story in the series examines how dire working conditions can become under the pressures of AI and automation. Refugees in Kenya are completing tasks for foreign technology companies under bizarre and opaque conditions.
The stories of desperate remote data workers used to highlight the low pay and horrid content they were exposed to. Today, workers who spoke to the Guardian say they aren’t even sure they will be paid, as their compensation is tied to a so-called “reward” system that decides whether they receive payment based on the quality of their work. Many of the workers called the system unfair but also said with dismay that they had few, if any, other options.
Read more: ‘Someone else will do it for less’: refugees in Kenya are powering tech for dwindling pay
The workers in Kenya also expressed a desperation to earn any money at these jobs before AI could carry out the rote tasks they were assigned.
Contrast these stories of unequal benefit with Sam Altman’s recent remarks on a podcast: “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.”
Altman was referring to the consequences of AI like the hack of Hugging Face or the attempted creation of bioweapons by would-be terrorists. Bad, to be sure, but lacking the moral outrage of human consequences.

OpenAI’s release of mathematical findings draws concerns from experts
